en: Preface to the *Record of the Efficacious Responses of Avalokiteśvara* The Great Being Avalokiteśvara is the master of the vast teaching and transformation of the Buddha-dharma. In the past, he already attained the realization of the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa;

yet, appearing in the world in reverse order, he manifests the form of a bodhisattva. He has established a great vow: until all sentient beings have been fully delivered, he shall not attain buddhahood.
The term "Bodhisattva" means one who awakens sentient beings. A "Mahāsattva Bodhisattva" means one who greatly awakens sentient beings.
He is called Avalokiteśvara because he observes the world; when sentient beings call upon his name, they all receive his salvation and are freed from suffering.
The name is established from the perspective of others' capacities (*parārtha*). Furthermore, regarding the title "Avalokiteśvara" (Contemplating the World):

it means that a single body manifests a thousand hands and eyes, responding and transforming according to the various classes of beings in a manner that is perfectly integrated and unimpeded; thus, the name is established from the perspective of one's own practice (*svārtha*). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Because my contemplation and hearing are perfectly luminous, the name 'Avalokiteśvara' pervades the worlds of the ten directions. One is able to use the faculty of the eye as the faculty of the ear, and so forth."
For these reasons, he is named Avalokiteśvara, the Unobstructed One. This Bodhisattva possesses the fourteen fearlessnesses, the thirty-two manifestations, and various supernormal powers.
When attending upon Amitābha, he serves as a close minister of Sukhāvatī;
when manifesting in the Sahā world, he acts as a worthy counselor to the World-Honored One. A single drop of water from his willow branch is sprinkled throughout the great trichiliocosm. Furthermore—
He has the deepest affinity with the sentient beings of this eastern land. All who wholeheartedly uphold his name, as well as the sutras and dharanis, shall accordingly receive his response;
it is not merely that his compassionate clouds cover only the southern seas.

Nevertheless, when sentient beings encounter times of suffering and difficulty, they immediately invoke the Bodhisattva to seek salvation; yet they must reflect that prior to this salvation from suffering and rescue from peril, there exists a Great...
The four characters for great kindness and great compassion reside [within the name]. If a bodhisattva does not rescue and deliver sentient beings, how can they be called a bodhisattva?

Yet, if one lacks great kindness and great compassion, regarding the suffering and hardship of sentient beings as if they were the fatness or leanness of a person from Qin or Yue—viewing them with such indifference that there is no concern—how could one be willing to seek their salvation?
If sentient beings merely mouth the title of "Bodhisattva" while being unable to possess the mind of a Bodhisattva, then...
If one lacks loving-kindness and compassion, being unable to save oneself first, how could one hope to evoke the compassion of the Bodhisattvas to rescue others from their suffering?
Is such a principle possible? Therefore, if people are free from treachery and the desire to kill, one's own mountain of blades will vanish.
If people are free from cruel and poisonous hearts, one's own cauldrons of boiling water and fires will be extinguished. If people are free from lack of loyalty and filial piety...
If one eliminates lustful greed and the lack of integrity, then one’s own hells will be exhausted.

If people are free from stinginess and jealousy, then the fires of the hungry ghosts will cease. If they are free from arrogance, stubbornness, and pride, then the evils of the asuras will be subdued.
If they are free from obstinacy and a lack of spiritual clarity, then the path of the animals will be far removed. As the Great Compassion Mantra says: "May all that is unwholesome be eliminated."
"Except for those who lack sincerity, it can be known that the recitation and upholding [of this mantra] require goodness and sincerity.
How earnest indeed were the words of the Tang-era Vice Commissioner! He said: 'All who reverently serve Avalokiteśvara must have deep faith in cause and effect;

throughout their lives, they do not create conditions for evil deeds, and thus their retribution for evil can be extinguished. I fear that people in the world merely know how to seek rescue from suffering..."
It is difficult. Yet, when one does not seek [the response] within a heart of compassion, and it fails to manifest even once, one then says, "The Great Being (Mahāsattva) did not grant a response.
Is this truly because the resonance between the Great Being and the world is empty and without evidence?
Therefore, I have compiled [this work] and written down these thoughts as a preface, hoping that people of the world may recite and uphold [the name of] Avalokiteśvara and hear of this together.

Late summer of the Jihai year of the Shunzhi era, Zhou Kefu, a disciple of the Pure Land practice at Jingxi, bathed himself in ritual purity and composed this "Preface for Encouraging the Circulation of Accounts of Efficacious Responses to the Recitation of Avalokiteśvara.
Wherever these scriptures reside, their circulation constitutes a virtuous condition; the resulting merit and retribution shall be immeasurable. Thus it is said: "One who is able to..."
Transmitting this Dharma-door to one person is equivalent to ten good deeds; transmitting it to ten people is equivalent to a hundred good deeds;

transmitting it to those of great nobility, great heroism, or great power is equivalent to a thousand good deeds; and carving new woodblocks for its wide distribution is equivalent to ten thousand good deeds.
How much more so for the Pure Land Dharma-door, which transcends the cycle of birth and death, ensures that one never regresses, and leads directly to the attainment of Buddhahood.
This encouragement for a single person to cultivate the Pure Land is precisely what brings one sentient being to the realization of Buddhahood.
All who attain Buddhahood must necessarily deliver immeasurable sentient beings; those beings whom they deliver all originate with me. Such is the karmic reward.

Faith is inexhaustible; therefore, I wish to exhort all who see and hear this to broaden their minds, taking the Buddha’s mind as their own, so that everyone may come to know it and be reborn in the Pure Land.
What Longshu has said should naturally be believed with earnest conviction as being without error.
As for the two sutras, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Avataṃsaka*, they are the most supreme among the wondrous teachings spoken by the Buddha.

The Great Being Avalokiteśvara universally delivers the world; there is no land where he does not manifest. The accounts of how past worthies were moved by his spiritual resonance are clearly evident throughout history.

I have compiled these individually to encourage those who cultivate their practice. This is truly a most expedient gateway—a bell and chime for those yet to come, and a bridge and raft for those on the final path.
In the autumn of the Wuxu year, I compiled the *Record of Experiences of Holding the Vajra*, which has already been circulated.

Preface. I respectfully entreat my fellow practitioners: I have now published these records concerning the Pure Land, the Lotus Sūtra, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, and the efficacious experiences of Avalokiteśvara’s recitation.

Having searched through various archives and verified accounts from both ancient and modern times, I have spared no small effort of mind and hand, intending to ensure that this devotion remains imperishable.
However, as the printing blocks for these works reside in Wumen, they have not yet been widely disseminated to other provinces. Since we all share in the adornment of the Dharma...
Within the Buddha-land, how could there be a lack of the supreme circulation of the Dharma? Furthermore, I address the faithful of the present age:
having obtained various editions, do not begrudge the effort to carve and distribute them extensively.

Whether following the original texts or revising them into new compilations, I especially hope that those who have witnessed or heard of accounts related to the efficacy of upholding [this practice] will continue to collect and record them hereafter. Even a single verse of praise is itself a [meritorious act].
To uphold the roots of goodness through the recitation of the name is to stir them in a single thought; this very stirring instantly eliminates karmic offenses.

In this way, one continues the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom, benefiting both oneself and others. As for the various deities who protect the Dharma, once they have protected the Treasure of the Dharma, they will certainly and unfailingly protect those who propagate the Dharma and carry its treasure.
In the past, the sages created "pictorial guides" (*kōzu*) to encourage people to practice *nien-fo*. Later—

Since others who practice mindfulness of the Buddha are mostly reborn in the Pure Land, one may attribute this merit to those who provide the illustrations; they too shall attain birth in the Pure Land.
The merit of the gift of Dharma is thus inconceivable. I vow to share this supreme benefit with all fellow beings.

During the Shining era of the Jin dynasty, the śramaṇa Zhu Fayi of Mount Shinan devoted himself to the meticulous study of the various scriptures. His disciples who received his instruction numbered over a hundred at all times.

In the second year of the Xian’an era, he was afflicted by a heart ailment; despite medical treatment, it proved ineffective, and he remained in a state of exhaustion and peril for many months. While Fayi was thus ill...

He constantly maintained mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara. Suddenly, he dreamed of a person who cut open his abdomen, removed his intestines and stomach to wash them clean, and then restored them to their place.
Upon waking, his illness was cured. Fu Liang, the Minister of the Secretariat during the Song dynasty, recorded this account, saying: "Chang said..."
"My late lord father associated with Master Yigong. Whenever he heard him speak of the miraculous manifestations of Guanyin, there were none among the listeners who did not respond with solemn faith.
(From the *Taiping guangji*) During the Yuexing era, the Śramaṇa Zhu Fachun of the Jin dynasty resided at Xianyi Temple in Shan-yin. He renovated the temple halls, building them anew.
He traveled to another town to purchase timber. As his boat passed through Lake Tai, evening fell and a violent wind arose; the waves were as high as mountains.
His vessel was small and water began to enter, leaving him in peril for a mere instant. He then focused his mind on reciting the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra to pray for divine protection.
Suddenly, a large ship drifted into view before him. They all climbed aboard by grasping its railing. Just as the last of the group had crossed over, he looked back toward—

The small boat had already capsized and sunk. The large boat was tossed and driven by the waves, reaching the shore in an instant. It was already night, and travelers had long since ceased their journey; how could this boat have arrived?
Truly, this was brought about by the supernatural power of a Bodhisattva. (From the *Fayuan zhulin*).
During the second year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, the monk Kai Da suffered a great famine. The Qiang and Hu barbarians were daily killing and eating people. Those who were harmed...
The number was beyond calculation. At that time, Da happened to be climbing a mound to gather licorice root when he was captured by the Qiang.

He was placed inside a stockade where more than ten people were already present; they had all been devoured by the Qiang. Once Da himself was taken captive, he silently recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra without ceasing.
When it was time for him to be executed the following day, at dawn, a tiger suddenly rushed toward the group of Qiang, roaring with fierce rage.

The tiger roared; the Qiang people were all struck with terror and fled. The tiger then bit through a section of the palisade until it formed a breach large enough for a person to pass, and then departed.

When Da first saw the tiger gnawing at the palisade, he thought he would certainly be harmed; however, once the breach was made and he found himself unable to enter, he began to suspect that something extraordinary was at hand.
He then escaped through a breach in the wall. Traveling by night and concealing himself by day, he eventually managed to escape.

(From the *Fayuan zhulin*). The Jin dynasty monk Shi Huiqian entered the monastic order in his youth. His observance of the precepts was precise and rigorous. During the Yixi era, he resided at Jiaxiang Temple in Shan-yin.

She disciplined her body and led the assembly in the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Later, as she lay ill, her thoughts were fixed upon the Land of Bliss, and she offered sincere prayers to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara).

At North Monastery, there was a nun named Jingyan, whose practice was profound and long-established. One night, she dreamed that the Great Being entered through the western city gate, his radiance shining brilliantly.
There were banners, streamers, and flower canopies adorned with the seven precious jewels. The nuns were struck with wonder and paid their respects, asking, "Where is the Bodhisattva going?
He replied, "I am going to Jiaxiang to welcome Master Qian. On that day, Qian’s countenance remained as usual, yet his attendants all smelled a rare fragrance.
He passed away peacefully (from the *Yunqi Wangsheng Ji*).

The Śramaṇa Fahong of the Jin dynasty resided at Waguan Temple. In the twelfth year of the Yixi era, as the government had prohibited smelting and casting, Fahong previously resolved to cast a sixteen-foot golden image.
Having no other choice, he completed the private casting; however, while the image was still in its mold, the authorities...
Zhi Jue arrested Hong and placed him in shackles. Hong focused his mind on Avalokiteśvara, reciting the name one hundred times every day.
Suddenly, he dreamed that the golden image he had cast went into the prison and rubbed the crown of Hong’s head with its hand, saying, "Have no anxiety; your misfortune shall soon be resolved.
On the chest of the image, an area about a foot square was copper-colored, appearing as if scorched and bubbling. Within ten days, a general amnesty was proclaimed, and Hong was released.
The image then broke through the mold and manifested itself (from the *Bianzheng lun*).
When the Jin dynasty monk Fazi was first about to leave the household life, he once traveled alone through a vast marsh when he suddenly encountered a fierce fire spreading and burning.
The flames reached him from all four sides; he knew that his death was certain. He did nothing but prostrate himself and recite the name of Avalokiteśvara. Suddenly the fire passed over him;
although not a single stalk of grass remained in the marsh, the fire did not reach the spot where Zhì had sheltered his body. Later, he became a general under Yao Xing.
While on a military expedition against the northern barbarians, he happened to lose his horse and fell into their encirclement.

He then hid himself amidst the thorny bushes by a ditch, continuing to invoke Avalokiteśvara with the utmost sincerity. When the barbarians arrived and searched for him, they could not find him anywhere;
thus he escaped. Thereupon, he resolved to renounce secular life and become a monk. (From the *Mingxiang ji*)
During the Yixi era, Shi Daotai of Changshan in the Jin dynasty once dreamed that someone told him, "Your life will end at forty-two.

Upon waking, Daotai was filled with fear. When he reached that age, he fell ill and resigned himself to his inevitable death. He distributed all the resources from his robes and alms bowl to perform meritorious deeds.
A friend said to him, "I have heard that making offerings to sixty-two billion bodhisattvas is equal to [making an offering to] one..."

The merit of reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara is identical and no different. Why do you not take refuge with a sincere heart? Your lifespan will surely be extended. Daotai was moved to realization;

he then devoted himself to the recitation for four days and nights, with single-minded diligence and without ceasing. Suddenly, beneath the curtain where he sat, a radiance entered from outside the door.
He saw Avalokiteśvara standing at a distance, the golden color between his feet and ankles shining brilliantly. Daotai hurriedly drew back [the curtain].

[The account of] the curtain-bowing ritual (*wei-kou-li*): Having performed it, he no longer saw [the apparition]. Startled and joyful, his sweat flowed; he immediately felt his body grow light, and his ailment was instantly cured.
He truly obtained longevity. (From *Guanyin Ganying*).
When the Jin dynasty śramaṇa Hongman was still a layman, he contracted a seasonal illness which caused both his legs to become cramped and paralyzed. He thought to himself:
Mǎn became an incapacitated person. He could do nothing but recite and contemplate the name of Avalokiteśvara morning and night, seeking deliverance.

Suddenly, he saw a monk standing before him holding a pure water jar. Mǎn asked, "From where have you come, Master? The monk replied, "I have come because you have constantly entreated me with such sincerity.
Your foot ailment can be removed; I shall treat it for you. Mǎn followed these words and sought healing. He felt only as though something were being pulled away from his knee.
A few-inch nail [was driven in], and he was subsequently cured.

(From *Shanyutang Bisheng*) Zhu Changshu of the Jin dynasty was originally from India. He made it his practice to specialize in reciting the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra. Later, he resided in the region of Wu.

When a fire broke out in the district, the houses of the neighboring dwellings, which were joined together, were all consumed by the flames. Changshu’s house was situated directly downwind; the force of the fire—

The fire raged fiercely. He extended his single-minded devotion and invoked Avalokiteśvara; in an instant, the wind shifted and the flames were extinguished. The entire town was struck with wonder and marvel.
At that time, there was a wicked youth who, astonished by this spiritual miracle, waited for a night of high winds to bind firewood and set it ablaze, intending to burn the temple down.
Four times he threw the torches, yet they were all extinguished. Only then did the youth’s heart break before the saintly power, and at dawn he prostrated himself, confessing his transgression.
Shu said: "What supernatural power do I possess? I have merely recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra constantly and without ceasing; whenever difficulties arose, I was immediately delivered from them.
(From the *Biànzhèng lùn*). Wang Min of Langye during the Jin dynasty had no sons. His wife once prayed earnestly to Guanshiyin to seek an heir. Later, while Min was on a journey...

While traveling, he encountered a Hu monk whom he revered deeply. The monk said, "When I die, I shall become your son. Not long after, the monk passed away, and Sengmin’s wife subsequently became pregnant.
When the child was born, as soon as he could speak, he understood the Sanskrit sounds of the Western Regions; his intelligence surpassed that of others.
His character and capacity were extraordinary; he was Wang Hongming, a Minister of State during the Jin dynasty. His childhood name was Alian.
He recounted the events of his previous life with vivid and distinct clarity (*from the Bianzheng lun*).
Lü Song, courtesy name Maogao, was a native of Yanzhou who resided in Shifeng County. To the south of the county there was a stream with a rapid current.
The banks were steep and winding like coils; moreover, there were many large boulders. Even those traveling by day felt a sense of peril and dread.
Once, Sòngfù was walking through the stream more than ten li from home when evening approached and a great wind and rain broke out.

The darkness was so profound that he could no longer distinguish east from west and resigned himself to drowning. He did nothing but turn his heart toward Avalokiteśvara and recite the name without ceasing. In a short while, a fire appeared.
The light reached the shore; it was as if someone were holding a torch, moving ten or more paces ahead of and behind the boat, illuminating the stream clearly so that he was able to return home.
Daosong always recounted such miraculous manifestations of the Bodhisattva to others. (From the *Fayuan zhulin*).
Dou Zhuan of the Jin dynasty was a native of Henei. During the Yonghe era, Cao Chang was the Regional Inspector of Bingzhou and Lü [Xun] was the Regional Inspector of Jizhou.
Huo [was in charge], and each of them led their own factions in discord. Zhuan was employed by Huo as a trusted official. Huo dispatched cavalry to launch a surprise attack, and Zhuan was captured.
Seven of his companions were also imprisoned together with him in a single jail; their shackles and fetters were extremely severe, and they were scheduled for execution on a fixed date.
At that time, the śramaṇa Zhidao Shan was in Huo’s camp; having previously known Zhuan, he heard of his imprisonment and went to visit him. Zhuan—
He said to Shan, "My life now hangs by a thread; can you save me? Shan replied, "If you can recite the name of Avalokiteśvara with a sincere heart, there will surely be a response.
Sengchuan then focused his mind on silent recitation for three days and nights. Suddenly, his shackles fell off of their own accord.
Thinking of his companions still in fetters, he could not bear to leave them alone. He again earnestly invoked the Bodhisattva’s divine power to provide universal salvation. When...
He said, "Let us both escape," and as soon as he finished speaking, the others were all liberated in succession. They then set out at night, opening the gates and departing;
they traveled through the outskirts without anyone noticing them. After traveling more than ten *li* beyond the city walls, dawn broke, and they took refuge together in a forest.
In a short while, pursuers went forth in all directions, searching almost everywhere, yet none ever reached the small plot of land where Huiquan and the others were hidden.
Thus they were able to escape the disaster. The group returned to their hometown, where everyone reverently practiced and believed in the Dharma.
Later, Daoshan crossed the river and recounted these events in detail for Xie Fu. (From the *Zhenzhuan Shiyi*).
Liu Du of Pingyuan was a native of Liaocheng. More than a thousand households in his home district all made offerings to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara.

He regularly recited scriptures and performed prostrations. At that time, he encountered the barbarian ruler Mulmo. Because fugitives from this county had frequently fled to him, Mulmo was greatly incensed and intended to slaughter the city.
The people were all filled with anxiety and fear. Sengdu then purified his sincerity and led the multitude to pray before the statue of Avalokiteśvara.
Not long after, while Zhimou was attending to his official duties, he suddenly saw an object descend from the air and circle the pillar of the house where he lived.

Startled, he looked closely and found it to be a single scroll of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra. He ordered it to be brought and read; Zhimou was greatly rejoiced and consequently reduced the infliction of punishments.
Thus, the entire city was spared from harm. (From the *Mingxiang ji*)
Xu Rong of Jin was a native of Langya. Once, while traveling back from Dongyang via Ding Mountain, his boatmen were unaccustomed to the waterways and mistakenly entered a whirlpool.
On the verge of sinking, Xu had no other recourse but to urgently invoke Avalokiteśvara. Within a short while, it was as if dozens of people were pulling the boat with all their might;
they leaped out of the whirlpool and descended along the riverbank. However, [the sky]— (Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)
The colors of the world had already grown dark; rain fell in torrents and the wind howled wildly, with white waves tossing toward the heavens. He knew not where he was headed.
Hui-rong cast both life and death aside and recited the sutras with single-minded devotion without ceasing. Suddenly, he saw a bright, penetrating light from the top of a mountain;

he rushed toward it and reached the shore directly. Once he arrived, the light was no longer to be seen. The next morning, he asked the people by the harbor, "Last night, what was that on the mountain?"
"What fire? the crowd asked in astonishment, saying, "With such wind and rain, how could there be fire? They then realized it was the secret protection of the Buddha’s power.
Later, Hui Rong served as the Commander-in-Chief of Kuaiji. Xie Fu once heard this account from him.

At that time, the śramaṇa Zhi Daoyun, who was traveling on the same boat as Rong, also recounted the matter in detail to Fu Liang; his account was identical to what Rong had related. (From *Fayuan zhulin*)

Lin: Zhang Chong of Jingzhao Duling was a man of the Jin dynasty. From his youth, he had served the Dharma. During the Taiyuan era, after Fu Jian’s defeat, the people of Chang’an fled in terror at the mere sight of the enemy winds.
At that time, Zhang Chong returned to the Jin, but he was detained by the garrison forces and identified as a marauding invader.
Fashong was bound hand and foot with shackles along with four companions and buried in a pit, each person twenty paces apart.
They were to be executed the following day. Fashong, realizing he would certainly die, focused his mind on purity and invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara.

In the middle of the night, his shackles suddenly broke of their own accord, allowing him to escape. On his way, he passed a temple where he again called upon the name of Avalokiteśvara and paid homage with a sincere heart.
He took up a stone and prayed, saying: "I now wish to cross the river eastward to petition the Emperor of Jin to rectify this grievance and save my wife and children.
If my heart's desire is to be fulfilled, may this stone split in two. As Sengchong bowed, the stone immediately split apart. He then proceeded to the capital.
He presented the "White Tiger Vessel" (Baihuzun) and detailed the circumstances of his grievances. The Emperor then granted him clemency.
Those who had already been abducted and sold by others were all redeemed by imperial decree and restored to the status of registered households. (From the *Fayuan zhulin*).
Nangong Ziao of the Jin dynasty was a native of Shiping; while on garrison duty at Xiping City, he was captured by the Feifei barbarians and taken to the Prince of Changle.
Those targeted for execution numbered several thousand throughout the city, all of whom were slaughtered. Ziao, knowing he could not escape, simply called upon Avalokiteśvara with a sincere heart.
When the executioners began their assault, a multitude of blades fell upon him simultaneously, yet they could not wound him. At that time, the Duke of Changle personally presided over the execution;
struck with amazement, he questioned him. Ziao did not know why this was so, and thus asked: "What abilities do you possess? Ziao then...

He replied, “I can make a horse saddle,” whereupon he was released. Thereafter, he fashioned a small image of the Buddha, enshrined it in a fragrant casket, and burned incense before it morning and evening to pay homage (from the *Mingxiang ji*).

Luan Xun, the Magistrate of Fuping during the Jin dynasty, had long been devoted to the Buddha-dharma. Once, while accompanying the military campaign against Lu Xun, his forces suffered a minor defeat in battle.
His boat was nearly destroyed by fire, and he was surrounded on all sides by a multitude of bandits. Being right in the middle of the river, the wind and waves were terrifying and strange;

Xun was filled with dread and felt certain that his death was inevitable. He chanted the name of Avalokiteśvara, when suddenly he saw a man standing tall and solitary in the midst of the river, his waist level with the water.
Xun knew in his heart that his prayer had been answered, so he leaped into the water to reach him. Once his body...
He floated up, his feet as if treading upon the ground; shortly thereafter, the main army dispatched boats to receive those who had been defeated, and he was thus able to escape.

(From the *Mingxiang ji*) Pan Daoxiu of Wu Commandery in the Jin dynasty was over twenty years old when he followed the army on a northern expedition. Having been defeated in battle, he was plundered and taken to a foreign land.
He sold his labor at several places and became a slave, unable to return home. Having long believed in the Buddha-dharma, he constantly invoked and meditated upon Avalokiteśvara amidst his perils.

In every dream, he would see the Bodhisattva standing before him. Later, seizing an opportunity, he fled southward until he reached a desolate mountain range where he was lost and knew not the way back.
Suddenly, in the midst of the sky, the Bodhisattva’s true form appeared—just like the walking image seen today—and pointed out the path for his return.

When Pan Zuoli had finished his work, he suddenly vanished from sight and was subsequently able to return to his own country. Thereafter, his diligent practice became even more earnest, and he passed away at the age of sixty.
(Recorded in the *Mingxiang ji*).
During the fourth year of the Taishi period of the Jin dynasty, Guo Xuanyi served as the Commandant (*simao*) for Yang Siping, who was the Regional Inspector (*zhizhi*) of Liangzhou. Yang...
Because he had harmed Fan Yuanzhi and others, Xuán was also imprisoned along with them.

He focused his mind solely on taking refuge in Avalokiteśvara, reverently reciting the Bodhisattva’s name day and night. One night, as he was about to sleep, he suddenly beheld the Bodhisattva manifesting his form, its radiance illuminating the prison.
He prostrated himself and prayed earnestly; after a long while, the vision vanished. Not long thereafter, Xuán alone received [the grace].
He received a pardon. He then painted the compassionate countenance he had seen and erected a vihāra, where he made offerings until the end of his life (as recorded in the *Guanyin Ganying*).

Xu Yigao of Lu in the state of Qin was a man who had faith in the Dharma from his youth; he served as a Minister of State under Fu Jian. Toward the end of Jian’s reign, warfare broke out like swarms of bees.
The bandits captured Fayi and intended to harm him; they buried both his feet and tied his hair to a tree. During the night, Fayi single-mindedly called upon Avalokiteśvara.
After a short while, he dreamed of a man who said to him, "Now the situation is urgent; do you still have leisure to sleep?
Startled awake, Fayi saw that his guards were all exhausted and asleep. He then attempted to move himself, and suddenly his hands and hair were released, as was his foot.

He managed to escape. He fled in haste for over a hundred paces and hid himself amidst the thick grass. When the pursuers arrived in full gallop, their torches forming a starry array, no one could see him.
At daybreak, the bandits dispersed; he returned to a temple in Ye and was thus spared.

(From *Mingxiang ji*) Bi Lan of Dongping in the Qin dynasty was a man who had long venerated Avalokiteśvara. Later, he followed Murong Chui on a northern expedition and fell captive among the barbarians.
Riding alone, he fled in haste; as the pursuers were about to overtake him, Lan invoked the name of the Bodhisattva with utmost sincerity and was ultimately able to escape.
He then entered deep into the mountains, where he became disoriented and lost his way. Again, with single-minded devotion, he turned toward the Buddha;
at midnight, he saw a monk in dharma robes holding a staff, who showed him the path, enabling him to return home. (From the *Mingxiang ji*)
Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty was preparing chicken eggs for his imperial meal when he suddenly heard a chorus of voices from within the cauldron chanting, "Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

Stricken with profound sorrow, the supervising cook reported this to the Emperor. He sent someone to investigate, and it was indeed so. The Emperor sighed, saying, "I did not know that the spiritual power of the Buddha-way could be such as this.
He issued an edict that from now on, chicken eggs were not to be used. (From the *Ganying pian zhuan*)
The Song dynasty monk Guṇabhadra was of royal lineage from Kaśmīra. He had deeply penetrated the Tripiṭaka and was extensively versed in the Mahāyāna.
During the Yuanjia era, he traveled east and resided at Qiyuan Monastery in Jinling. Nanqiao Wang Yixuan and others all took him as their teacher.

The Prince assembled more than seven hundred śramaṇas specializing in doctrinal studies with the intention of lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, but the Master [Guṇabhadra] felt that it had not yet been fully transmitted.
Huayan felt deep shame and admiration. Consequently, he performed prostrations and repentance morning and evening, reverently praying to Avalokiteśvara for a hidden response.
Suddenly, one night, he dreamed of a divine being holding a sword and exchanging his head with that of another person.

Upon waking, he suddenly understood the Huayan language without impediment. He subsequently lectured upon it more than ten times, and his listeners were moved to submission. Emperor Wen once asked him:
The Emperor said, "I wish to observe the precepts and refrain from killing, yet as the ruler of a state, I am unable to fulfill this aspiration. What should I do?
The Master replied, "The cultivation of a sovereign differs from that of a commoner. A commoner has a lowly station and little renown; he must therefore exert his will and practice self-mastery."
The Emperor takes the four seas as his home and the myriad people as his children. When he utters a single virtuous word, scholars and commoners alike rejoice;

when he implements a single benevolent policy, humans and spirits are brought into harmony. When punishments do not cut short life and corvée labor does not exhaust strength, then wind and rain come in season, cold and heat are regulated, and the hundred grains flourish.
To observe the fast in such a manner—truly great is the fast! To refrain from killing in such a manner—truly great is the precept!
This too is the ultimate [path]. Why wait until one reduces a meal for a single day or saves the life of a single creature before one can achieve great salvation?

The Emperor struck his desk and praised this as excellent. He issued an edict for the relevant authorities to provide offerings, and the entire nation venerated him (as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
At the beginning of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema of Huanglong recited the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* and cultivated ascetic practices with pure devotion.

Accompanied by twenty-five followers, he traveled far to visit the land of the Buddha. Having endured many hardships and perils, as he was about to reach Śrāvastī in India, he encountered a herd of wild elephants on the road.
He recited the sutras from memory and invoked the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion; thereupon, a lion emerged from the forest.
A herd of wild elephants bolted away. Furthermore, a wild ox arrived bellowing, intending to cause harm.
[The practitioner] again took refuge as before. Suddenly, a large vulture was seen flying toward him; the ox, likewise startled, fled. (From the *Fayuan zhulin*).

The Song dynasty śramaṇa Zhu Huìqìng was a native of Guangling. His practice and study of the scriptures were refined and clear. In the twelfth year of the Yuánjiā era, [he was active in] Jingzhou and Yangzhou.
During a great flood, Huìqǐng was about to enter Lúshān. When his boat reached the river, a violent wind suddenly arose.

While the fellow travelers had already managed to take refuge on the shore, only Huìqǐng’s boat drifted in the middle of the river; the wind was fierce and the waves surged, making it certain that the vessel would sink.
Huìqǐng settled his mind and sincerely recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra. Those on the bank saw his boat and, braving the gale, cut through the current to reach him.
It is like when several dozen people pull a boat toward the shore until the entire vessel is safely rescued.

(From the *Fayuan zhulin*). Shi Daojiong of the Song dynasty was a native of Fufeng. While his master Daoyi was ill, he and four companions entered Mount Huo in Henan to collect stalactites (*zhongru*).
After exploring the cavern for several li, they encountered a deep stream. They crossed it by laying a wooden beam across, and Daojiong was the first to cross. The others...

They all drowned. The torches were extinguished once more. Sengjiong silently recited the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Samantamukha-parivarta*), praying with sincere devotion for deliverance while keeping Avalokiteśvara in mind.
Suddenly, he saw a light like fireflies; in a short while, it shone brightly throughout the cave, and he was finally able to find a path out.

In the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era, when the Prince of Linchuan was stationed at Guangling, he invited Sengjiong to serve as his preceptor. In the ninth month, he performed a ten-day period of contemplation.
At Yinzhai, on the ninth day at the fourth watch of the night, while the assembly of monks were all asleep, Sengjiong rose to prostrate himself.

Just as he was about to sit in meditation, he suddenly saw countless śramaṇas upon the four walls, all appearing with only their upper bodies visible. Within them was a Buddha, whose snail-shell curls were clearly and distinctly manifest.
A majestic man, holding a long sword in his hand and possessing an extremely heroic and extraordinary countenance, pressed incense into Jiong’s hands and said to him: "You..."
Keishu (可受) was able to receive incense and protect his host; he then vanished in an instant.

Later, during a feast for Samantabhadra, two monks came to prostrate before the Buddha and flew away through the air upon leaving the gate. The assembly was all struck with wonder and amazement. (From the *Fayuan zhulin*).
As for the śramaṇa Huihe of the Song dynasty, he was a monk at Zhongzao Temple in the capital. During the persecutions of the Yuanjia era, He still served as a "white-robed" [lay practitioner].
Yi was under the command of Liu Hu. Hu frequently dispatched several dozen officers and soldiers as spies, and He also participated among them.
When they reached Quezhu, they encountered the imperial army advancing from the west; the group of spies fled and scattered.

He escaped to Xinlin, where he exchanged his tunic and trousers for the tattered clothes of a country elder and assumed the guise of a farmer. Carrying a basket and a load on his back, he walked along at that time when various roaming troops were present.

The surveillance and interrogation were extremely strict. The interrogators observed Huo’s facial expressions and, becoming suspicious, questioned him. Huo’s answers were somewhat evasive, and he was captured and brought before the executioner for decapitation.
As Huo fled on his own, he recited the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* with all his might. When it came time for the execution, his prayers became even more earnest.

Soon after, when the soldiers raised their blades, they repeatedly missed their mark; three times they struck, and three times the blades broke. The military commander was startled and released him. Thereupon, Huo...
He left the household life and subsequently achieved mastery in his religious practice.
(From the *Fayuan zhulin*) Shi Tanyi of Changgan Temple during the Song dynasty was a native of Kuaiji. He entered the monastic order in his youth and strictly observed the precepts.

He could recite over one hundred thousand words of scripture; his chanting was clear and resonant, naturally peerless. He constantly suffered from ringworm, which persisted despite prolonged treatment. His room...
He made offerings to an image of Avalokiteśvara and prostrated morning and evening, praying for the healing of this ailment.

One day, he suddenly saw a snake climb onto the roof and a rat fall to the ground, its body covered in saliva and foam as if it were already dead. While waiting for the rat to revive, Ling took a bamboo scraper and cleared away the saliva and foam.
He then heard that a rat swallowed by a snake could cure skin sores; he consequently applied the saliva to his ringworm, whereupon the rat immediately...
He recovered. Within two nights, his sores and ailments were suddenly gone. Only then did he realize that the snake and the rat had appeared because of his sincere prayers.
Subsequently, his fame spread far and wide, and the ruler of the state provided him with offerings.
(From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*) Sun Daode of Yizhou in the Song dynasty was originally a Daoist priest (*jijiu*). He was over fifty years old and still had no son. He lived...
Near a monastery, during the Jingping era, a monk said to him, "If you can sincerely prostrate and recite the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra, you may hope for a son.
His grandson followed this advice. One day he had a strange dream, and his wife indeed became pregnant and gave birth to a boy. (From *Mingxiang ji*).
Wang Qiu, style name Shuda, a native of Taiyuan, served as the Governor of Fuling. In the first year of the Yuanjia era, while [he was] there...

The commandery fell into enemy hands, and he was imprisoned. His cell was secured with sturdy locks. Qiu had long been a devoted follower of Śākyamuni and, while serving as an official, had always loved the people.

Upon reaching the prison, he saw more than a hundred men, most of whom were starving. At every meal, he would share his portion with them. He maintained a fast daily and recited the name of Avalokiteśvara with a sincere heart.
One night, he dreamed that he ascended a high seat and saw a śramaṇa give him a scroll of a sūtra; its title was inscribed as "Guang" (Light).
He was clearly reading the "Chapter on Receiving and Practicing," along with the names of various bodhisattvas, when he forgot the name of the first bodhisattva.
The second was Avalokiteśvara, and the third was Mahāsthāmaprāpta. He also saw a chariot wheel; a śramaṇa said, "This is the gate to the five realms of existence.

Upon waking, his shackles were all severed and fallen away. Qiu knew in his heart that this was due to supernatural power, which further increased his single-minded devotion. Thereupon, he drove nails into himself.
He was placed in shackles, but after three days, he was pardoned. (From the *Fayuan zhulin*). Wang Xuemu of the Song dynasty was a native of Taiyuan.
During the Yuanjia era, he lost his command while leading a northern expedition. Xiao Bin intended to execute him, but Shen Qingzhi remonstrated, saying:
"Fuli (the childhood name of Emperor Shizu of the Wei dynasty) has a prestige that shakes the world; how could Xuemu possibly withstand him? Furthermore—"
"To kill the generals would only weaken our own ranks," he said, and so he desisted. Initially, when Xuānmù was about to be executed, he dreamed that someone told him:
"If you can recite the 'Universal Gate Chapter' and the 'Great Compassion Mantra' of Avalokiteśvara one thousand times, you may be spared. Upon waking, he recited them without ceasing.
Suddenly, it was reported that the execution had been stayed. Later, his official rank reached that of Kaifu (Grand Marshal). (From the *Fahua Gantong Zhuan*).
Zhang Xing of Xinzheng, during the Song dynasty, was a man who, in his daily life, placed his faith in the Buddha. He once received the Eight Precepts from the śramaṇas Tanyi and Sengrong.
Later, he was falsely implicated by bandits; while Xing fled, they seized his wife and imprisoned her. Subsequently, the county authorities placed her under detention.

A fire broke out. Prisoners were led outside. It happened that Daorong and Daoyi were walking together past the side of the prisoners. The wife [of one prisoner] cried out, "Upādhyāya, why do you not save me?
Daorong said, "I, this poor monk, have no power to save you. I pray that you will diligently recite the name of Avalokiteśvara;
perhaps you may then obtain release. The wife then prayed and recited day and night. After about ten days had passed, she suddenly dreamed of a śramaṇa at night who, with...
He kicked her and said, "Get up, get up! His wife immediately started in alarm and rose; her shackles were all loosened.

However, the door was still closed, and the guards were so strict that she could not leave for fear of being discovered. She returned to her bed with her chains and fetters back on and fell asleep again.
Once more he dreamed that a śramaṇa called out to her, "The door is already open. Upon waking, his wife ran out; the guards were all fast asleep. There was no one there.

As for the one who knew: while traveling several li through the darkness, he suddenly encountered a man. His wife was startled and terrified, falling prostrate to the ground. Upon questioning him, it turned out to be her husband.
They supported each other amidst a mixture of grief and joy, and quickly sought refuge in the place where the monk Yi was hiding; thus, they managed to escape with their lives.
This concerns events from the early years of the Yuanjia era (recorded in the *Guanyin Ganying*).
Bian Yuezhi of the Song dynasty was a native of Jiyin. He held the rank of Chaoling; at the age of fifty, he still had no son, so his wife took a concubine for him.
Furthermore, she had long been barren and prayed for an heir. She made a vow to recite the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* one thousand times;
when the count was nearly complete, she conceived and subsequently gave birth to a son. This occurred in the fourteenth year of the Yuanjia era (as recorded in the *Mingxiang ji*).
Zhang Chang of the Song dynasty constantly upheld the practice of Avalokiteśvara. When the Prince of Nanqiao plotted a rebellion, Chang refused to comply. The Prince intended—
He was about to kill him. At night, he dreamed that Guanyin said to him, "You must not harm Chang. Thereupon, he did not dare to kill him. When the king was defeated, Chang was imprisoned.
He recited the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* one thousand times; the shackles broke inch by inch. The jailer replaced them, but they broke again.
The official reported this, and he was released. (From the *Tansou*)

Fu Wanshou of Pingchang lived during the Song dynasty. In the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era, while serving as a military aide to the Guard at Guangling, he requested leave to return to his home commandery.
At the beginning of the fourth watch, as he crossed the river, the long waves flowed peacefully; by the middle watch, however, a wind arose like an arrow.
The darkness was so profound that they knew not which way to turn. Wanshou took refuge in the Dharma, single-mindedly taking refuge in Avalokiteśvara, his recitation never ceasing from his lips.
Suddenly, he and those on board the ship together beheld a light upon the northern shore, appearing like a village fire.
He turned his boat and hurried toward it, arriving before dawn. He questioned those on the opposite bank, and they all said that as the watch had ended, there was no one lighting fires.
Only then did he realize it was the power of the Buddha.

(From the *Fayuan zhulin*) As for Che Mu of the Song dynasty, her son encountered the disaster at Qingni during the time of the Prince of Luling and was captured by the barbarians, falling into their hands.

In the camp, his mother remained at home and had long been a devoted follower of the Buddha. She lit seven lamps before the Buddha and, throughout the night, focused her mind on Avalokiteśvara, praying that her son might escape.
This she continued for years. Eventually, seizing an opportunity, the son fled southward; he hid by day and traveled by night, alone and disoriented as to his direction.
Each time he saw seven trails of light ahead, he suspected they were villages and wished to hasten toward them to seek refuge.
[He] tried to reach [her], but in the end could not do so. Thus it continued for seven days and nights; before he realized it, he had arrived home.
He saw his mother still prostrating before the Buddha in dedication, with seven lamps blazing brightly. Only then did he realize the prior cause and know it was the power of the Buddha.
Mother and son were reunited, and they took refuge [in the Triple Gem] for the rest of their lives. (From the *Xuanyan ji*)
Qi Pengzijo was a native of Yiyang. He left home to become a monk in his youth, but returned to lay life and continued to recite the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* every day.
In the first year of the Jianyuan era, he served as the County Clerk of his home commandery. Having been imprisoned for an offense, the Prefect Shen Wenlong was determined to execute him;

his shackles and restraints were extremely severe. Pengzijo was filled with anxiety and fear, yet had no other recourse but to recite the sūtra with utmost sincerity until he had completed more than one hundred recitations.
Exhausted, he fell asleep during the day. There was also Du Daorong, an official from Xiangxi County, who was imprisoned with him.
As he drifted between sleep and wakefulness, he suddenly saw two white cranes fly and alight beside Ziqiao; his feet were already free from their shackles.
Startled, he rose to look, and Ziqiao had also awakened. Daorong then told him what he had seen. Ziqiao realized that the Buddha was protecting him and that this ordeal would surely be resolved.
Furthermore, fearing that the prison authorities might suspect him of intending to defect, he was placed in shackles. After five days had passed, he was released. (From the *Fayuan zhulin*).
Li Rujun, the commander of a military unit stationed at Hulao, was surrounded by the Wei invaders. In a desperate situation, he intended to surrender; thus, he scaled the city wall at night.
He went out and saw the bandits lying scattered and prostrate. Ju-run then single-mindedly invoked Avalokiteśvara and passed through the bandit camp.

Some bandits followed after him; Ju-run hid himself within a thicket of grass and trees. When the bandit horde suddenly arrived, Ju-run was overcome with terror, yet he focused his mind solely on reciting the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra.
Suddenly, he found a horse and galloped away. (From the *Bianzheng lun*)
Lu Hui of Wu was imprisoned and faced the certainty of death. He therefore ordered his family to create an image of Avalokiteśvara and prayed for his life to be spared.

When he was led to the execution ground, three blades were used one after another, yet each blade broke. An official questioned him, and he replied, "I suspect this is due to the compassionate power of Avalokiteśvara.
Upon examining the statue, it was found that there were three knife marks upon its neck. Consequently, the case was reported to the throne and he was granted clemency. (From the *Xuanyan ji*)
Gao Xun of Huanyang was already fifty years old when he committed murder and was cast into the dungeon in chains.
His fellow prisoners urged him to exert himself and together recite the name of Avalokiteśvara. Xun replied, "My crime is so grave; how could I possibly be spared?

Although his fellow prisoners urged him repeatedly, it was only then that he resolved his mind, vowing to abandon evil and practice goodness, and to focus single-mindedly on Avalokiteśvara. He prayed that if he were granted a fortunate escape...

He vowed to construct a five-story stupa and offered himself as a slave to provide for the Sangha. For ten days and nights, he applied his mind with such sincere devotion that his shackles and chains fell away of their own accord.
The supervising official was struck with wonder and said to Xun, "If the Buddha has compassion for you, even if you were executed, you would not die."
On the day he was to be executed, as the executioner raised his blade, it snapped in two. When the Emperor heard of this, he granted him a pardon (*Xuanyan ji*).

Shi Jun was a man of exceptional literary talent, yet he revered the Daoist path while treating Buddhism with contempt. He would often say to others, "The Buddha is a barbarian deity; there is no need to serve him.

Whenever he saw images of the Honored One, he would invariably mock them with derision. Later, both his feet became afflicted with a contraction that prevented him from leaving his bed. A physician... [text ends]
His prayers proved entirely ineffective. A friend, Zhao Wenwei, said to him, "This illness cannot be saved unless one possesses great compassion and power.

Try to give rise to a resolute mind and cast an image of Avalokiteśvara; if you pray to it, you will surely receive a response. Because his illness was so urgent, Liu Jun followed these words and had an image cast.

When the image was completed, he suddenly dreamed that Avalokiteśvara descended into his chamber. Consequently, he recovered from his illness. Because of this, Yuan Jun repented his transgressions and came to believe in the Dharma.
(From the *Xuanyan ji*) During the Wei dynasty, the śramaṇa Daoji was traveling in the Western Mountains of Shouyang when he was captured by bandits. They bound him to a tree, intending to kill him.
He focused his mindfulness on Avalokiteśvara and maintained this until death without ceasing. When the bandits drew their blades, they struck him repeatedly, yet he suffered no injury.
The bandits fled in terror, and thus he was able to escape. Furthermore, the śramaṇa Fachan encountered bandits while traveling in the mountains;

he did nothing but recollect Avalokiteśvara. The bandits drew their bows and shot at him, but the arrows could not wound him. They eventually cast their bows to the ground and submitted with sincere devotion. (From *Guānyīn Gǎnyìng*).
During the Jiemin era of the Wei dynasty, Lu Jingyuan served as a National University Doctor (Guozibo). Incriminated on a charge, he was imprisoned in the prison of Jinyang.

With single-minded devotion, he recited the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Pumenpin*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*; with his remaining strength, he also recited the entire scripture. Suddenly, his shackles fell off of their own accord.
The official in charge reported this to the court, and he was granted a special pardon. (From the *Fahua Gantong Zhuan*).
During the Tiānpíng era of the Eastern Wei, Sūn Jìngdé was a recruited soldier in Dìngzhōu who upheld the teachings of Śākyamuni.
He once fashioned an image of Avalokiteśvara and personally offered it his veneration. Later, he was implicated by bandits and could not withstand the torture.

Suddenly, he dreamed of a śramaṇa who instructed him to recite the name of Guǎnkū Āguānshìyīn one thousand times. As he approached execution, he completed the full number of recitations; the blade broke spontaneously into two pieces.
His skin and neck were not wounded. He changed his blade three times, and the result was the same each time. His superiors reported this matter in a formal memorial.

The Chancellor Gao Huan submitted a petition requesting that he be exempted from death. Upon returning home, he saw that there were three knife marks on the neck of an Avalokiteśvara image (from the *Xuánxiáng jì*).
During the Northern Zhou dynasty, the monk Huìgōng of Zhāotí Temple in Yīzhōu formed a pact with his fellow student Huìyuǎn; later, they traveled...

Huiyuan returned from Jingzhou and Yangzhou after seeking the Way. For thirty years, he had been a close friend to Huirun. During a night conversation, Huiyuan’s speech flowed like a stream, while the Master remained silent with no response.
Huiyuan said, “Why not recite a sutra? The Master replied, “I only recite one scroll of the ‘Universal Gate’ chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
I shall recite it for you; just listen with a sincere heart. Thereupon, he established an altar, ascended the high seat, and began to chant aloud.
The title of the scripture: It was as if there were a fragrant aroma. After a long while, the sound of celestial music was heard shaking the void, and flowers rained down in profusion.
Only after the recitation of the scripture had concluded did it cease. Huiyuan paid his respects and thanked him with reverence. (From the *Fahua Gantong*).
At the beginning of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, there was a monk from Yangzhou whose name has been lost. He could recite the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* by heart and took pride in his mastery. Qí...
A novice monk from Mount Dongshan in the prefecture was reciting the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra when both he and a fellow monk died suddenly.

When they arrived at the Netherworld, the King seated the novice on a golden throne and treated him with great respect, whereas he placed the *nirvāṇa-saṃgha* (the other monk) on a silver seat, showing him somewhat less deference.

The monk felt aggrieved and asked the novice where his residence was. Upon reviving, [the monk] traveled south to Qifu, where he found the novice and inquired about the matter. The novice said: [The rest of the narrative follows.]
"Whenever I opened the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, I invariably wore clean robes, burned famous incense, and recited it only after completing my prayers. I have never dared to be negligent.
The monk apologized, saying, "My transgressions are deep. In my recitation of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, my deportment was not orderly, and my body and mind were not yet pure."

This is the reason for the variations in the degree of reverence shown by the King of the Underworld. (From the *Fayuan zhulin*). Emperor Wenzong of the Tang dynasty was fond of clams. For many years, they were presented as tribute from the southeastern coastal regions, causing the people unbearable suffering. One day, [The text continues: ...the Emperor dreamed that he was being summoned by the King of the Underworld. Upon waking, he felt a sense of dread. He then issued an edict prohibiting the collection of clams for several years, and the people’s hardships were thereby alleviated. This account illustrates how the King of the Underworld can manifest his power through dreams to influence the affairs of the world. It is said that the spirits of the dead possess knowledge of both the past and the future; thus, one must not treat them with contempt.
