The imperial kitchen obtained a giant clam that could not be split open with a knife; when tapped, it opened. Inside was the Sanskrit-form image of Avalokiteśvara.
The Emperor was struck with amazement and ordered it to be enshrined in a sandalwood casket adorned with gold. Later, he questioned Chan Master Weizheng, who said:
"Things do not respond in vain; this has merely opened Your Majesty’s mind to faith, so that you may practice frugality and love the people. The Master continued, "The Sūtra says:
'If one is to be saved by means of a Bodhisattva body, the Buddha will manifest as a Bodhisattva body and preach the Dharma for them.

The Emperor said, 'I have seen the Bodhisattva body, but I have not heard him preach the Dharma. The Master asked, 'Does Your Majesty believe this? The Emperor replied, 'How could I dare not believe it? The Master said:"
When the Emperor had thus heard the conclusion of his preaching, he was greatly delighted and attained awakening.

He forever abstained from eating clams and consequently issued an edict for every monastery throughout the realm to establish an image of Avalokiteśvara; this is the origin of [the practice at] Mount Potalaka. (From the *Guanyin Ganying*).
The Tang dynasty śramaṇa Xuanzang, surnamed Chen, was a native of Yanshi County. From childhood, he was intelligent and possessed virtuous conduct. At the beginning of the Wude era...

Having received imperial edict to travel to the Western Regions to retrieve the scriptures, Xuanzang reached the kingdom of Jibin. The roads were perilous and impassable, leaving him with no means of proceeding.
He then locked himself in an empty room and sat there. At dusk, he opened the door and saw an old monk sitting alone upon a couch;
his entire body was covered in sores, festering with pus and blood, and he did not know from where the man had come. Xuanzang prostrated himself and made a fervent plea to the monk. The monk—
He orally transmitted one scroll of the *Heart Sūtra* and had Xuanzang recite it.

Consequently, the mountains and rivers became level and easy to traverse, the roads were cleared and opened, tigers and leopards hid their forms, and malevolent spirits and demons vanished from sight. He reached the Buddha-land, where he obtained over six hundred sūtras before returning home.
The *Heart Sūtra* has been transmitted to this day. Initially, when Xuanzang was about to depart for the Western Regions, there was a pine tree at Lingyan Temple.
Xuanzang stood in the courtyard, rubbed its branch with his hand, and said: "I am going west to seek the Buddha-dharma; you may point toward the west.
If I return, you shall turn back toward the east, so that my disciples may know of it. When he departed, that branch pointed westward year after year.
It originally pointed westward and measured several *zhang* in length. One year, it suddenly turned east; the disciples said, "The Master has returned," and they went west to welcome him.
Indeed, Xuanzang did return. To this day, this pine tree is called the "Blessing-Pine" (*mó-dǐng-sōng*).

(From the *Táng xīnyǔ*) Master Wanhui of the Tang dynasty was a native of Méngxiāng. His secular surname was Zhāng. Initially, his mother prayed to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara before conceiving Hui.

Hui returned to life, but he was dull-witted. Only when he was eight or nine years old could he speak; his parents raised him like a piglet or a puppy. When he grew older, his father ordered him to plow the fields.
Hui would simply plow straight ahead for several li without turning back. He would stop only upon encountering a ditch or a pit, while constantly repeating the word "equality" (*pingdeng*).
His father became angry and struck him. Hui said, "Both sides are plowing; why must there be such difference? Hui.
His elder brother was stationed far away on military duty at Anxi, and news from him had been cut off for a long time. His parents believed he was dead; they wept in sorrow day and night.
Returning home, [the son] felt deep pain for his parents and knelt, saying: "It is now of no benefit to weep in worry for my brother.
I calculate that what he requires are clothing and provisions; please prepare these with haste. I shall await him. One morning at dawn, he informed his parents and set out. By evening—
He immediately returned home and said, "My elder brother is quite well. He had a letter for his parents; upon reading it, they saw that it was indeed his brother's handwriting.
The entire family marveled at this. From Hongnong to Anxi is over ten thousand *li*, yet he had returned from those ten thousand *li* in a single day.

Therefore, he was titled "Wanhui" (Ten Thousand Returns). Previously, when Xuanzang was traveling to the Buddha-land to retrieve scriptures, he saw an inscription on a pillar at a Buddhist shrine that read:
"The Bodhisattva Wanhui has been banished to Mianxiang to spread the transformative teachings. Xuanzang hastened by post-station to Mianxiang to visit Wanhui;
he paid him homage as his teacher and departed after presenting him with the three robes, a water jar, and an alms bowl. (From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*)
The Great Master Saṃgha of Tang was a man from the Western Regions, surnamed He. At the beginning of the Longshuo era, he came to travel in this land.
In the Xinyi Ward of Linhuai County in Sizhou, he requested a plot of land and erected a marker, intending to establish a monastery.

Beneath the marker, they unearthed an ancient inscription for Xiangji Temple along with a golden statue, upon which were inscribed the characters "Buddha King Universal Radiance" (Puzhao Wang Fo). Thereupon, the temple was constructed.

In the second year of the Jinglong era, Emperor Zhongzong dispatched an envoy to welcome the Master into the palace and honored him as National Teacher. Shortly thereafter, he departed and resided at Jianfu Monastery.
He habitually stayed alone in a single room; there was a cavity on the crown of his head which he constantly plugged with cotton wool, but would remove the wool at night.
Fragrance issued from the crown of his head, its sweet scent being extraordinary. At dawn, the fragrance returned to enter the crown of his head. The Master frequently washed his feet;

when people took that water and drank it, their chronic illnesses were all cured. One day, the Emperor spoke to the Master in the inner palace, saying, "The capital region has had no rain for several months.
I pray you will show compassion and dispel my anxiety. The Master then poured water from his flask, sprinkling it into the air. In an instant—
Dark clouds suddenly arose, and a refreshing rain fell heavily. The Emperor was greatly pleased and issued an edict bestowing a plaque for the temple he had commissioned.

The Master requested that it be named "Puzhao Wang" (Universal Illumination King), but the Emperor wished to avoid the imperial taboo name of the Empress Dowager; thus, it was changed to "Puguang Wang" (Universal Radiance King).

He then personally inscribed the plaque with his own brush and bestowed it upon the monastery. On the second day of the third month in the fourth year of the Jinglong era, at Jianfu Temple in Chang’an, [the Master]... end.
He passed away while seated. The Emperor immediately ordered a stupa to be built within the monastery and his lacquered body to be enshrined there for veneration.

Suddenly, a great wind arose, and a foul odor pervaded Chang’an. When the Emperor asked for the reason, a close minister reported: "The Great Master Saṃgha’s karmic conditions for transformation lie in Linhuai;
he likely wishes to return there, which is why this portent has appeared. The Emperor silently gave his consent in his heart, and the foul odor ceased instantly. Shortly thereafter—
For a moment, a wondrous fragrance wafted intensely. In the fifth month of that same year, he was sent to Linhuai, where his stupa remains to this day.
Later, Emperor Zhongzong asked Wanhui, "Who was Master Saṃgha? Wanhui replied, "He was an emanation of Avalokiteśvara.
It is as stated in the *Universal Gate Chapter*: "Those who should be saved by the form of a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, or other such forms..."
He manifested all these [visions] and preached the Dharma for them; this is what is meant by that. When the Master first arrived in Chang’an, Wan Hui paid his respects with great reverence.
The Master patted his head and said, "Young man, why have you stayed so long? You may go now. Not many months after the Master passed away, Wan Hui also died.
The Master’s traces of transformation were numerous; they are recorded in full in his original biography. (From the *Jiwen lu*)
The Tang dynasty monk Huiri boarded a sea vessel and reached India to visit learned masters and inquire about the essential teachings of the shortcut path.
Upon arriving at the kingdom of Gandhāra, he found a statue of Avalokiteśvara on a great mountain to the northeast; there, the Master prostrated himself for seven days while abstaining from food.
He set a deadline for his life’s end. On the seventh night, he suddenly saw Avalokiteśvara manifest in a body of purple-gold, seated upon a precious lotus flower.

The Bodhisattva extended his hand to touch the master’s head and said, "If you wish to transmit the Dharma to benefit yourself and others, nothing surpasses the practice of mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
Having spoken, the figure suddenly vanished. The Master returned to Chang’an and, consequently, exhorted everyone [to practice this].
He practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name. (From *Dinglianyu Dianshang*).
The Tang dynasty monk Zizhao resided in Zhenzhou and constantly made this vow: "I vow that through Avalokiteśvara, I shall behold Amitābha Buddha."
Thereupon, he cast a statue of Avalokiteśvara forty-nine feet in height. Once it was completed, he made a vow with a sincere heart.

At the third watch of the night, two streaks of golden light suddenly appeared; he saw the Buddha descend from within the light, with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta following on his left and right.
The Buddha extended his hand and touched Huijue’s crown, saying: "Firmly maintain your vow without wavering; prioritize benefiting all beings. This shall be your place of birth in the Jewel Pond."
Who could have wished otherwise? Eleven years later, on the evening of the full moon in the seventh month, he saw a person whose form was like that of a celestial king, manifesting amidst the clouds.
This being said to Jue, "The time for rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing has arrived.
He then sat cross-legged before the statue of Avalokiteśvara and passed away (from the *Wǎngshēng jí*).
During the Kaiyuan era, the monk Daoxian of Shengshan Temple in the Tang dynasty resided at Dayun Temple in Jiangzhou, where his fellow practitioners held him in high esteem.
At that time, the Regional Inspector Yuan [surname lost] wished to have seven scrolls of Avalokiteśvara painted and entrusted the task to Daoxian because of his disciplined conduct.

Daoxian ordered the painters to observe the *zhāijì* (fasting and purification) before applying their brushes; furthermore, he had all the pigments mixed with *rǒutóuxiāng* (stallion-head incense) instead of glue, ensuring the utmost solemnity and purity.
Yan Yuanshen praised him highly. When the work was finished, he went to Yuning to cut timber for rafting to build the Mañjuśrī Hall.

As the raft was about to return, it suddenly capsized in the water. The river current was swift and turbulent; his companions wished to rescue him but could not reach him in time. At the moment Xian fell into the water—
He then called to mind Avalokiteśvara and saw a strange light at the bottom of the water; the seven painted bodhisattvas all appeared before him.
They said to Xian, "Simply recite 'Namo Amitābha Buddha,' and this calamity will be resolved. In a moment, he emerged from the water.

His robes and sandals did not get wet. Today, the seven bodhisattva statues at Dayun Temple still exist, and they include painted depictions of the incident of falling into the water to record this marvel (*Guang yiji*).

Shi Zhiyi of the Tang dynasty was a native of Changsha; his surname was Wu. He had formerly served as a soldier in the campaign against the Man tribes and was by nature fond of fishing and hunting. Because he... [text fragment ends]
There was a white tortoise; he boiled it and ate it, whereupon his entire body broke out in sores that all became festering and putrid.
His eyebrows, whiskers, and the fingers of his hands and feet fell off until nothing remained. Crying out in pain, he did not die immediately, and he went about begging in the markets of Annam.
A monk saw him and took pity on him, saying to him: "You should turn your mind back toward Avalokiteśvara and recite the Great Compassion Mantra; I shall orally transmit it to you."
"If one can apply oneself with diligence, one will surely obtain a favorable retribution. He finally accepted these words and recited them single-mindedly.

From that time on, his sores gradually healed and his fingers all grew back. Once he had fully recovered, he shaved his head to become a monk and established a vihāra in the former residence of General Fu Ba to reside there. (From the *Taiping guangji*)
Tang’s Cen Wénběn, courtesy name Jǐngrén, was a native of Jíyáng. From his youth, he had faith in Buddhism and recited the *Púmén pǐn* (Universal Gate Chapter).
Once, while traveling by boat across the Wú River, the vessel capsized in midstream and everyone was drowned. Wénběn also sank into the water;
suddenly, he heard a voice say, "Since you can recite the *Púmén pǐn*, you shall surely escape this water disaster. This occurred three times, whereupon he floated to the surface of the water. He...
He arrived at the shore after some time. One day, while he was hosting a vegetarian feast at his home, a monk arrived late and said to him, "The world is currently in turmoil;
by virtue of your wholesome roots, you have fortunately escaped the calamity and shall eventually encounter a period of peace, attaining wealth and nobility.

Having spoken, the monk vanished. When the meal was concluded, two śarīras were found in his bowl. Later, he served the Tang dynasty as Grand Secretary (Zhongshu Ling). (From the *Fahua Gantong Zhuan*)
During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, Xu Shancai, a native of Liquan, regularly observed the precepts and recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra more than several thousand times.
Once, he went to Yanxing Temple in the capital to perform meritorious deeds.

On his way back, he encountered Hu rebels who were leading away captured Han people toward Hongya to execute them. Realizing he could not escape, Shancai did nothing but recite the name of Avalokiteśvara with urgency.
The Sūtra states: At the moment he was about to be killed, he was completely unaware of it.

It was not until nightfall that he realized his body was atop the branch of a tree in a deep ravine, more than three hundred feet from the precipice. He rubbed the crown of his head with his hand; feeling a slight sting, he found no injury.

Gradually descending the tree, he followed the southern bank of the ravine for about several tens of li. When day broke, he was already far removed from the bandits. Finding the path, he returned home. Master Wǎn once...
This account is related [in the *Fayuan zhulin*].

During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, Dong Xiong of Henan served as the Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review. He was implicated in the case of Li Xianton and consequently incurred the Emperor’s wrath.

The Imperial Attendant Wei Cong was dispatched to interrogate him with great urgency. Li Jingxuan of the Court of Judicial Review and Wang Xin, a Rectifier of the Law, along with dozens of others, were all imprisoned together.
Xiong focused his mind exclusively on the *Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter), reciting it thirty times every day without ceasing even at night.
The shackles and chains suddenly loosened of their own accord. Startled, he informed the guards. That night, the Censor-in-Chief Zhang Shouyi was on duty;

he personally inspected them and found it most extraordinary. He re-secured the locks with a strict seal and departed. Sengxiong continued his recitation of the sutras, and at the fifth watch, the locks loosened once again.
When it hit the ground, there was a sound, yet the seal and title remained as they were. Those who heard of this, both inside and outside the palace, marveled at it.
When the matter was settled, the prisoners sharing his cell were all granted their freedom.

(From the *Fayuan zhulin*). Du Zhikai of the Tang dynasty was a native of Jiyin. From his youth, he took pleasure in the Buddhist scriptures; he did not serve in office nor did he marry. Wearing monastic robes, he lived in seclusion.
Taishan made the recitation and chanting of scriptures his primary practice. In the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era, he returned from the mountains and suddenly fell ill, nearing death.
He covered his body with his *kāṣāya* robe and, in a state of profound stupor as if dreaming, saw some ten or so women repeatedly coming to disturb him.
Zhikai remained upright and unmoving; they gradually drew closer and approached him, saying they wished to seize Zhikai and cast him away to the north.
In a mountain stream, there was someone clutching a *kāṣāya* robe who suddenly chanted the Buddha’s name in unison, then withdrew to repent and requested that an Amitābha Buddha be fashioned for him.
He recited the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva more than thirty times.
After a short while, he felt a profuse sweat break out over his body and was cured. (From the *Fayuan zhulin*)
During the Linde era of the Tang dynasty, Xu Yan of Yongxing Ward in the capital made his living by catching fish. Later, he fell ill and died in a state of profound suffering;
his body was red as fire, and the pain exceeded that of being cauterized with burning coals. He said that he saw only chariot-fires coming to burn his body.

A minister of the underworld rebuked him for the heavy karma of his fishing profession and sent him back to undergo punishment in his present life. Several days had already passed, during which he repeatedly revived and died.
His relatives urged him to perform meritorious deeds, so he had two statues of Avalokiteśvara made, which he venerated and used for repentance;
he also ordered his entire family to observe a vegetarian diet. Before long, his illness was cured. (From the *Fayuan zhulin*).

During the early Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, Cheng Gui served as a district magistrate (*wei*) in Changsha. He was sent to transport timber for the Henan Bridge; upon first arriving in Yangzhou, he fell ill.
Encountering wind and waves, they lost a great many items. The local authorities suspected him of theft and sale, subjecting him to interrogations that were unbearable.

He falsely confessed to having squandered them. The authorities then sent a formal notice to the provincial government of Tan. At that time, Ban Jingqian was a stern and vigilant official in the Tan administration.
He dispatched the inspector Yang Jin to Yangzhou to arrest Guī. Jin, wishing to extort bribes, subjected him to illegal torture and coercion, placing shackles and a collar upon him.
The ship's beams were nailed shut on all four sides, with only small holes opened to pass food through. Guī felt certain that he would surely die upon reaching the prefectural seat.
From the day he departed Yangzhou, he resolved his mind to invoke Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, the Savior from Suffering, and maintained a practice of eating only once every day.
He either fasted or drank only water while observing a pure retreat for over ten days.
Upon reaching Chukou, he chanted with such earnest devotion that his shackles suddenly opened of their own accord. He waited until late at night when the boatmen were all asleep;
he removed the nails, climbed out of the hold, and called out to Jing, saying, "What will you do with me? Startled, Jing rose and asked, "How did you get here? Gui replied, "I would rather—"
"To be buried within the belly of a river fish—how could I have wished to die at the hands of you lot? He then leapt into the water.
Upon first reaching the bottom of the river, he encountered a floating log; clinging to it, he managed to float to the surface. Driven by the waves, he was carried to a reed beach.
At daybreak, he entered a village, where the residents escorted him to Chuzhou. The local officials were all struck with amazement and provided him with travel gear and provisions for his journey.
He urged Guī to enter the capital to petition the Censorate regarding his grievance. Once Guī had departed for the audience, [Wáng Qí’s] followers dispersed all at once;
for this reason, he too entered the monastic order. (From the *Jìyìjì*).
Wáng Qí of the Táng dynasty was a native of Dàyuán who resided in Xíngyáng. From his childhood, he abstained from meat and blood. At the beginning of the Dàlì era, he became...
The District Magistrate of Accounts (Sihu) of Quzhou was by nature fond of reciting the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra. From his youth until his maturity, he frequently suffered from serious illnesses;
yet every time he chanted the sūtra, he would recover. Furthermore, while reciting, there were often ghosts of strange forms and exotic species who came to disturb and harass him.
Because his mind was upright and sincere, [the deity] could not violate him; thus he brought about his own eradication [of misfortune]. (From the *Guang yiji*).
A scholar from Hengyang during the Tang dynasty was advanced in years and had no sons. He prayed for an heir without exhausting any means. Suddenly, he encountered an old monk.

He bestowed upon them the *Baiyi Guanyin Jing* (The Sutra of White-Robed Avalokiteśvara), saying, "The Buddha taught that whoever can receive and uphold this sutra will obtain immeasurable merit according to their heart's wishes.
If you seek a son, you shall immediately give birth to a wise male child. There was a peculiarity regarding the white robes being wrapped in layers.

Thereupon, the husband and wife recited it with utmost sincerity until they had completed one entire collection (*piṭaka*). After several years, they subsequently gave birth to three sons; indeed, it came to pass.
The layman Baiyi (White-Robed One) wrapped [the image] in layers. The Governor of Hengyang personally witnessed this event and reprinted it for distribution, also praying for the birth of an heir.
Within a year, he fathered a son. (From the *Baiyi Jingji Yan*).
During the Tang dynasty, Zheng Lin, a military clerk in Raozhou, died and arrived at the Netherworld. The King examined the registers and, knowing that he had been summoned in error, released him.

He returned and said to him: "Return to the human realm and strive diligently to do good. When you see someone killing a living being, simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;
they will attain rebirth [in the Pure Land], and you too shall gain merit. (From the *Longshu Jingtuzhuan*, citing the "Responsive Manifestations of Avalokiteśvara")
Ouyang Can of Tang was a native of Xuzhou. He had long been devoted to the recitation of the Avalokiteśvara and Mahākaruṇā Dhāraṇīs.
His home was fifty *li* south of the prefectural city. Once, during the summer months, he entered the city and did not return until dusk.

That evening the sky was dark and overcast; after traveling about twenty *li*, a torrential rainstorm broke out. Halfway along the road, there were mountains and forests flanking the path, with dense shade and deep valleys. Previously—
There were many fierce beasts, and Baochan’s heart pounded incessantly. Once he had reached the mountain path, the rain grew even more torrential.
Suddenly, a massive creature appeared before him, over ten feet long and white in color; its head and feet could not be distinguished at all. It was barely ten paces away.
He did not part from his companion. Chan was greatly terrified and wished to recite the Great Compassion Mantra, relying on the power of the Bodhisattva to ward off the threat;
however, his mouth was so clenched that he could not produce a sound. He could only keep it in mind and recite silently. After several repetitions, he was finally able to chant aloud clearly.
As he continued chanting without ceasing, the monster suddenly vanished, and the rain also subsided somewhat. Thus, he was able to reach home. (From *Yutang Xianhua*)

Meng Zhijian of the Tang dynasty was a native of Bingzhou. When he was young, he fell ill and suddenly passed away. He saw the government offices as they usually were; at that time, no one knew he was dead.

He encountered an old acquaintance who served as an official there, who asked him, "By what means have you come here? Meng told him everything in detail, whereupon he first realized that the place he had reached was the realm of the underworld.
The official consulted the registers and said, "In your lifetime, you accumulated no merit through almsgiving or good deeds. How have you managed to return? Meng Zhijian...
He said, "Throughout my life, I have recited the Heart Sūtra and the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra; though I do not recall the exact count, it amounts to approximately thirty or forty thousand recitations.
The official then indeed searched for him and, having informed the Lord of the Netherworld, he was released and returned. The official asked, "Do you wish to know your future destiny?"

He then showed him the register. On it was recorded that Zhi Jian had been appointed as a *chushen* (official by recruitment) to transport grain; he served as a *canjun* (military aide) in Caozhou and was subsequently transferred to serve as a *sicang* (granary clerk) in Dengzhou.
[Zhi Jian] immediately concealed the document and refused to let him see it, leading him instead into a dark pit. He thus survived.

He did not know what the "transporting grain" (*yun*) referred to, but soon there was an imperial decree recruiting for grain transport, and consequently, he was selected and appointed as the *canjun* of Caozhou, then transferred to the post of *sicang* in Dengzhou.
He departed from his post and was subsequently selected as a magistrate of Jinzhou, but died before he could arrive there (*from the Chaoye Qianzai*).

Li Xin of the Tang dynasty was skilled at reciting the Thousand-Handed, Thousand-Eyed Dharani. There was a man suffering from malaria; Xin recited the mantra for him, and the demon manifested its form.
It said to the man, "I originally intended to greatly distress and humiliate you, but because I fear Master Li Shisi, I did not dare do so."

"Come! Fourteen Lang is none other than Xin. Xin’s family resides in Dongjun, but he has been traveling as a guest in Henan. His younger sister fell ill and died several days ago, but she has returned to life.
She said: 'At first, I was led into a tomb by several people. One among them said, "This is the younger sister of Li Shisi (Fourteen Lang).

She is now returning from Henan and is about to arrive home. She is a virtuous person; if you hear my voice...'"* *(Note: The sentence regarding the voice appears to be incomplete in the source text.)*
[The deity] seized his younger sister, thinking, "He will surely distress us with divine incantations; it is better that we return her quickly.
Once the girl was restored to life, Han Xun also arrived at his residence. (From the *Guang yiji*).

During the Tang dynasty, Han Guangzuo, the Magistrate of Taolin, traveled with his family to take up his official post. On the way, he passed by the temple of Mount Hua and dismounted from his carriage to pay his respects.

While he was entering the ancestral temple, his favorite concubine suddenly died. He ordered a shaman to petition the deity. The shaman said, "The Third Lord wishes to take your concubine for himself.
Although you have petitioned him, she has been spared for now; however, when you reach your post in the county, he shall certainly take her.

Upon arriving at his post, Guanzuo summoned a goldsmith and had a golden image of Avalokiteśvara cast for the sake of his concubine, seeking to escape this calamity. Five days later, the concubine again died suddenly; it was not until half a day later that...
Sū said, "Just now, the Lord of Mount Hua arrived with a full retinue of carriages and horses to welcome me. As I was leaving the gate, a golden-colored monk appeared before them.
The carriage and its attendants were struck with awe and did not dare to pass; consequently, they dispersed. From this, Guāngzuò’s faith in the Inner Teaching (Buddhism) grew even stronger.
(From the *Jiwen*):

The Woman of Ma Village in Tang originated from the region west of Shan. Previously, the local custom in this area was to practice horsemanship and archery, and they were unaware of the names of the Three Jewels.
In the twelfth year of the Yuanhe era, a beautiful woman suddenly appeared, carrying a basket to sell fish; people vied with one another to marry her.
The woman said, "If there is one who can recite the *Universal Gate Chapter* (*Pumen pin*) in a single night, I shall take him as my husband.
At dawn, more than twenty people were able to recite it. She then gave them the *Diamond Sutra* (*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*), and ten were still able to recite it.

She then gave them the entire *Lotus Sutra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*) and set a three-day deadline for mastery. Only the son of the Ma family was able to do so; she then prepared the rites and welcomed him home.
Upon entering, the woman feigned illness and requested to stay in a separate room. A short while later, she died; her body immediately began to rot and decay, and she was subsequently buried.
After several days, an elderly monk wearing purple robes arrived at the burial site and ordered the grave to be opened for inspection. Inside, there were only golden-linked bones.
He said to the assembly, "This is the Great Being Avalokiteśvara. Out of compassion for you all, who possess heavy karmic obstructions, he has manifested this through skillful means."
"I have merely transformed you. Having spoken these words, she flew through the air and departed. (From the Preface to the Portrait Eulogy of Song Qianxi.

Zhang Shi, the wife of Chen Xuānfan of the Tang dynasty, devoted her heart to the service of the Buddha. She constantly vowed to commission a statue of Avalokiteśvara and to provide lifelong offerings to it.
Because her strength was insufficient to fulfill this, she focused her mind on the goal for many days. Suddenly, a golden image of Avalokiteśvara appeared, its radiance brilliant and resplendent.

It was magnificent. Measuring about five feet in length, it appeared upon a high seat, leading the assembly to marvel at how such a response was brought about by refined spiritual resonance (*jinggan*).
(From the *Bianzheng lun*) A single scroll of the *Heart Sūtra* in golden characters, handwritten by Li Houzhu of Southern Tang, was bestowed upon his concubine, Lady Qiao.

Later, when it entered the inner palace of Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty, she heard of Houzhu’s death and took the sūtra out from the inner quarters to offer it to Xiangguo Temple as a merit-making offering for the deceased.

Dedication. Furthermore, she wrote this herself at the end, saying: "The former consort of the late Emperor Li, Lady Qiao, on the occasion of the hundredth day of the Sovereign’s passing, respectfully donates one scroll of the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*—originally written by her when she was a concubine—to the West Pagoda Cloister of Xiangguo Temple.
She prays that before Maitreya Buddha, she may behold the Buddha while holding a single flower," and so forth. Later, Jiang...
A monk from the South brought it back to his native country and placed it within the *cakra* (spire) of the pagoda at Tianti Temple. Later, a great fire broke out in the temple;
although the *cakra* fell from the midst of the flames, the scripture was not damaged.
(From the *Mojì*; *Guanshiyin Chiyàn Jì*, Vol. 1).
*Record of the Miraculous Responses of Avalokiteśvara*, Part II:
Shi Zunshi of Song, surnamed Ye, of Taizhou. His mother made earnest prayers to the Ancient Avalokiteśvara and gave birth to the Master.
At eighteen, he shaved his head; first, he studied the Vinaya at Chanlin Temple, and subsequently entered Guoqing Temple, where he burned off a finger before the image of Samantabhadra.
Formerly, he vowed to transmit the Tiantai teachings. His learning was profound and his ascetic practice rigorous; his fame surpassed that of others throughout the two provinces of Zhejiang.

He studied the doctrinal and contemplative systems extensively and dedicated himself solely to rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). He once practiced the *Banzhou sanmei* (Pratyutpanna Samādhi) with a period of ninety days.

Having long suffered from vomiting blood due to his studies, the skin of both his feet cracked while he remained within the meditation hall. The Master made a vow of death to himself. One day, as if in a dream, he saw a white...
The monk Yigan saw Avalokiteśvara lower his hand and point toward his mouth, drawing out several worms. Again, nectar issued from the tip of the finger and was poured into his mouth;

upon consuming it, his body and mind became cool and refreshed. From that time on, his chronic illness was suddenly cured. This account appears in the *Chanyan ji*. His cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) rose more than an inch above his head.
His two hands hung down past his knees, and his voice was like a great bell; these were all different from before, so that the assembly all sighed in admiration and veneration.

The Master founded several hundred rooms for the Tianzhu Monastery and constructed a Hall for the Guangming Repentance Rite. For every rafters he set up and every bricks he laid, he would invariably recite the Great Compassion Mantra seven times.
Though the monastery suffered three successive invasions by bandits, the fires were extinguished on their own each time, due to the firmness of his vow-power.

He attracted over a hundred disciples and thousands of students. He focused exclusively on the Pure Land, exhorting others to practice it, and authored the *Pure Land Resolving Doubts* (*Jingtu jueyi*) and the *Two Gates of Practice and Vows* (*Xingyuan ermen*).
Furthermore, his various liturgical manuals for the *Pure Land Repentance*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, and Avalokiteśvara were circulated throughout the world.
In the tenth year of the Tiānshèng era, he passed away while seated in meditation at the age of sixty-nine. The assembly witnessed a great star fall from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Feng was then known as the Patriarch of Repentance, Ciyun (as recorded in the *Lianzong baojian*).
When Fan Zhongyan, the Duke Wenzheng of the Song dynasty, was residing in Suzhou, his mother passed away. On the twenty-first day after her death, he dreamed that she wept and told him:

"Because I committed karmic offenses during my life in the world of the living, I have been detained by the Lord of Mount Tai and am undergoing punishments beyond endurance. My son has always been filial."

He requested that the entire *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* be recited to rescue his mother from her transgressions. The official woke up crying in alarm; he immediately purified himself through ritual bathing and invited a community of monastics to Mount Xuemu.
They chanted the sutra for seven days. As the period of prostrations and repentance was nearly complete, his mother appeared again in a dream and said:

"Because of your sincere prostrations and recitations, you have moved the Great Being clad in white (Avalokiteśvara) to descend among the common folk. He has held half a scroll of the sutra for me; now my mother not only—"

"Your sins will be extinguished, and you shall be reborn in heaven. The next morning, the son entered the sutra hall and inquired about this; he understood it for himself and thought, "I ought to offer a generous donation as a reward to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara).
Having finished speaking, he departed. On the following morning, the official prepared the offerings and paid his respects to the assembly of monks, after which he asked:

"Who among the assembly is one who holds even half a fascicle of this sutra? The assembly all turned pale with alarm. He replied, "As for the scripture I venerate, not a single character has been omitted;
how could there be such a thing as holding only half a fascicle? To his side, a monk spoke calmly:

"Yesterday, when the great assembly was reciting the sutra, I stood leaning against a pillar observing them. When we reached the sixteenth division, suddenly a Great Being arrived and took up [the scroll]."

The monk Xiang then returned to the kitchen to attend to his duties. Upon receiving the inquiry, he answered with frank candor. The official immediately prostrated himself in deep obeisance and reverently offered a donation (*dakṣiṇā*).
The monk said, "No, no," and suddenly ascended into the air until he vanished from sight. Among both the monastic and lay communities, there was none who did not gaze up in veneration.
Consequently, the official established the "No, No" Meditation Hall (*Momo Chan Tang*) to commemorate this miraculous event; it remains intact to this day. (From the *Jingang Lingying*).
During the Xuanhe era of the Song dynasty, Zhang Qing of Bianjing served as a jailer. He always maintained himself with compassion and prudence.

Rising at dawn, he would sweep away filth and impurities, being especially diligent during the hot months. Regarding food, drink, medicinal decoctions, and bedding, he invariably ensured they were refined and pure.

He would often admonish his subordinates, saying: "When people unfortunately fall victim to the law, if we do not show them pity and care, how can those who suffer punishment find any way to escape their fate?"

He appealed [for mercy]. Throughout his life, he had maintained the practice of reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*. Whenever he encountered a major crime that resulted in execution, he would invariably observe a month of vegetarian fasting and recite the sūtra before the matter was concluded.
He once instructed the prisoners: "If you have committed a crime, you should confess it yourself; do not falsely incriminate the innocent and good, thereby increasing your own karmic retribution.
His wife, Lady Yuan, died of an epidemic at the age of forty-eight. Three days later, she suddenly revived and said: "When I first arrived..."
She was in a foul place, longing for a cool and pure spot. Suddenly she saw the Great Being in white robes (Baiyi Dashi), who said to her, "You ought not to have come here;
moreover, you do not yet have an heir. Your husband has performed many deeds of hidden virtue, and among his descendants there shall surely be one who prospers.

He then took her by the hand and led her out, whereupon she regained consciousness. The following year she gave birth to a son, who attained an official post as a Class Three Jiezhi. In the eighth year of Qingli...
12. He passed away without illness. His six grandsons all achieved prominent official careers.

(From the *Ganying pian zhuan*) Zhai Jie, a native of the capital of the Song dynasty, lived in Sian Town in Huzhou. At the age of fifty, he had no son. He painted an image of Avalokiteśvara and prayed with utmost devotion.
While his wife was pregnant, she dreamed of a woman dressed in white who presented her with a child on a tray; the child’s appearance was exceptionally handsome and elegant.
He wished to take him in his arms, but a bull stood blocking the way between them, so that he could not reach him. After the boy was born, he died before the month was out.
He prayed with even greater devotion, and someone who had heard of his dream told him: "Your son craved beef; could this be the reason?

Jie was struck with awe and vowed that his entire family would never eat beef again. Thereupon, he dreamed once more that the woman from before brought the child to him; and indeed, [the child survived].

A son was born who later attained high status and distinction. Examining the case, it appears that although the Great Being (Mahāsattva) delivered the child, he ultimately became an obstacle for a single ox.

Was it that the Great Being’s supernatural power was inferior to that of a single ox? In truth, it was simply that the power of that person’s wholesome merit could not withstand the force of their evil karma.
In the end, he repented his misdeeds and ultimately obtained a son; thus, the compassionate and spiritual manifestations of the Great Being were even more marvelous.
Therefore, purifying one’s heart and reforming one’s faults is the very ground for receiving salvation.

(From "Turning the Wheel of Kalpas") During the Xuanhe era of the Song dynasty, Yu Jí of Lishui was traveling by boat with his family on their way to take up his post as a magistrate of Xinghua. On the banks of the Huai River, there were many...

There were oysters and clams; the boatmen bought them daily for food. Whenever Fayi saw them, he would buy them and release them into the river. Once, he happened to see a basket that was exceptionally heavy.
The group wished to cook and eat its contents, but Fayi refused to sell it even at double the price.

They then placed it in a cauldron. Suddenly, a great sound rose from within the cauldron, and flames surged upward. The boatmen were terrified, but when they opened it to look, a large oyster had split open, and between its shells—
He manifested an image of the World-Honored One with two bamboo poles placed beside it. Its marks and signs were dignified and majestic;

its robes, cap, necklaces, and even the bamboo leaves and stalks were all fashioned from fine pearls. He gathered everyone on board to recite the Buddha’s repentance for their transgressions, then took the shell home to enshrine and venerate it. (From the *Ganying pian zhuan*)
In the third month of the Wuchen year of the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, Shi Haoguo, Prince of Yue, was first serving as a magistrate in Yuyao.
Accompanied by Cheng Xiufu of Poyang, he went to Chaoyin Cave to pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, seeking a spiritual response. At first, there was utter silence and nothing was seen.
At the hour of *bú* (the late afternoon), they returned; a monk pointed out to them, "At the summit of the cliff there is a crevice from which one can look down. They climbed up and reached it.
As he looked back and forth, a miraculous sign suddenly appeared: a golden light shone brilliantly, and his features became clearly visible.
Toward evening, an elderly monk came to visit him and said, "From this appointment onward, you will pass through various high and important offices until you become a Grand Preceptor (Taishi).
This is a favorable outcome for Wen Lugu. When you serve as Prime Minister in the future, if the Emperor intends to wage war, you must earnestly advise against it."
"Twenty years hence, we shall meet as a high official and a prime minister in Yue. Having said this, he took his leave; upon exiting the gate, he suddenly vanished without a trace.
In the year Wuzi of the Qiandao era, when the former Prime Minister was stationed in Yue, one night a man of the Way appeared with a spirit and countenance of extraordinary refinement.
Claiming to have been an old acquaintance of the Chancellor, the gatekeeper refused to admit him. Thereupon, the visitor demanded paper and wrote in large characters: "Lu Xiang, black-headed."
The scenery of ten thousand li was redoubled. A blue-eyed barbarian monk had once shared a night of pure conversation with him; having cast down his brush, he departed.

Greatly astonished and amazed, [Zhaozhou] ordered him to be pursued, but though they searched everywhere, he could not be found. Recalling past events at Potalaka, he finally realized that this practitioner was none other than the old monk from those days.
At the end of the Chunxi era of the Song dynasty, a foot soldier named Yang Liang fell ill in Jianchang. He saw two officials holding warrants who were pursuing him;
Liang went out with them and was soon brought before an official. The official asked, "What meritorious deeds did you perform while alive?

Liang replied, "I served in the labor of running errands; whenever I was assigned a task, I never dared to miss the deadline. The official said, "I do not ask about that matter. There is something else..."
"What meritorious deeds did you perform? Liang then realized he was in the underworld and said, "I have merely recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra.
He asked again, "Since you have recited the sūtra, what good deeds have you ever performed? He replied, "I am but a lowly person; how could I have a single deed worthy of praise?
I simply know to abide by my lot and refrain from harming others. The King ordered the registers to be inspected, and it was as he had said; thus, he was granted rebirth. (From *Shanyutang*)

According to the *Bisheng* (Supplementary Notes), Lai Shenggan, a native of Jianning during the Song dynasty, was renowned throughout the realm. He habitually employed demonic arts, killing people to sacrifice to spirits.
He frequently sought out girls of ten or more years of age in Zhejiang to keep for his own use; his mother, however, delighted in reciting the Buddha’s name.
The woman followed his instructions and practiced reciting the Heart Sūtra. Subsequently, when it was her turn for the ritual sacrifice, she bathed and adorned herself, then entered an empty room;
he locked the door and departed. The woman, certain that she would surely die, recited the sūtra with single-minded devotion.
At midnight, she felt something emerge from beneath the skylight, its radiance shimmering brilliantly. Terrified, she hurriedly recited the *gate* mantra. Suddenly, from within the woman’s mouth—

A light emerged from it. The creature hesitated, wishing to advance but repeatedly retreating. After a long while, the light in its mouth gradually grew larger and shot forth at the creature with a metallic *keng* sound;
the creature fell prostrate to the ground. The room was near a street, and a night patrol soldier happened to pass by. The woman cried out loudly, "Kill me!
The soldier reported this to his superiors, who led a crowd to break down the wall and take the woman. They found a large white python lying dead there. It was captured.

The crime extended to his family members as well. Upon interrogation, they confessed their guilt; consequently, they were branded with penal marks and exiled to the frontiers, and their property was confiscated.
This residence is now the home of General-in-Chief Zhan (Tán-sǒu).
During the Song dynasty, Zhang Xiaochun had a grandson of five years who could not walk. Someone said to him: "Recently, in the region between Huai and Dian..."
A farmer had suffered from a chronic ailment of his legs and feet for a very long time. He simply maintained the recitation of the name of Avalokiteśvara every day without ceasing.
Consequently, he was moved by the manifestation of Avalokiteśvara, who left behind these four lines of verse: "The Great Wisdom arises from the mind; within the mind, there is nothing to be sought.
It accomplishes all meanings; it is neither ancient nor modern. The farmer recited this verse for a full hundred days, and his chronic illness was suddenly cured.
Xiaochun subsequently instructed her grandson and her wet nurse to observe the fasts and recite [the mantra] for three months; yet their gait remained as usual.
Those who suffered from ailments of the legs and feet all found efficacy through this recitation.
(From the *Bicheng*) Lady Li of the Song dynasty was renowned for her virtuous character. An old woman named Li came to her home carrying pearls and seeking to sell them.
After she had departed, the pearl was left behind on the ground. The Countess picked it up and wondered why the old woman had not returned for so long.
One day she arrived again, her appearance emaciated and vastly different from before. When the Countess asked the reason, she replied: "The pearl I sold was lost on my way back home.

The original owner has been pressing me incessantly for its return; though I have exhausted my family's resources, I cannot repay the debt. I have become ill from the weight of this anxiety and distress, and am nearly at the end of my strength."

She arose. The County Lady said, "The pearl was left behind by you at that time," and she immediately took it and returned it. The old woman was overjoyed beyond all expectation and offered endless prayers of thanks.
Later, the County Lady fell ill and was on the verge of death. She dreamed of a person in blue robes driving a carriage out into the wilds, arriving at a great official residence.
There she saw two magnificent figures sitting loftily upon high seats; they questioned her regarding her surname and name, whereupon the County Lady realized it was the underworld.
The official had habitually recited the Great Compassion Mantra (Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī) during his daily routine; he subsequently began to recite it silently.

The corridors and halls shook incessantly, and those around him were all struck with terror, nearly falling over. A majestic figure stood up and said, "Do not recite. We shall release you and let you go.
The official brought the registers and documents to his desk. The majestic figure asked, "Do you remember the matter of returning the pearl to Lady Li? The District Magistrate replied, "I do. One.
The scribe said, "I shall increase your lifespan by twenty years. One of the women replied, "Do not grant it too much.
The scribe said, "It is already difficult for a woman to love jewels and, with a clouded heart, covet wealth; how much more so when she possesses the merit of upholding this sutra!
He immediately ordered a servant in green robes to escort her back. The Lady returned to her carriage, arrived at the gate, and entered. There she saw—
Her corpse lay within the curtained tent while her family wept around it; suddenly she awoke, and her illness was subsequently cured.
Later, she indeed lived for twenty years before passing away. (From the *Ganying pian zengzhu*).
Lü Hong, a Court Official of the Ministry of Works during the Song dynasty, and his wife, Lady Wu, both observed the precepts and practiced pure cultivation, attaining clear awakening.

Regarding Buddhist principles: Wu Qian served Avalokiteśvara with such devotion that he experienced spiritual responses. Whenever he was in a purified chamber, he would arrange dozens of jars and pots and fill them with water.
Holding a willow branch in his hand, he recited mantras; each time, he would see Avalokiteśvara emit light that entered the jars and pots.
Those suffering from illness were often cured by drinking the water consecrated with mantras. This water remained undeteriorated for many years and did not freeze even in extreme cold;
thus, the world called her "Lady Guanyin. She had two female attendants who also cultivated pure practices.

One of them observed the precepts with rigorous austerity, sometimes fasting for an entire month, consuming nothing but a single cup of the pure water of Guanyin consecrated by Wu each day. After some time, she suddenly beheld the Buddha.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva was present before her eyes, and after three years, she attained rebirth there.

(From *Longshu Jingtu Wen*) Li, the mother of Dong from Dexing County of the Song dynasty, recited the *Pumenpin* for over thirty years. Later, she entered the underworld and saw Avalokiteśvara extending his hand to lead her away;
his radiance was like daylight. He said: "Your allotted lifespan has already ended, but because you possess roots of goodness, [I have come to guide you]."
She came to transmit [the teachings] to her, and she revived suddenly and completely. (From the *Fahua Gantong Zhuan*).

A daughter of the Wang family from Jixian during the Song dynasty recited the "Universal Gate Chapter" of the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, as well as various sūtras such as the *Amitābha* and *Vajracchedikā*.

She recited the Buddha’s name seeking deliverance. After her mother had died and been coffined, blood flowed profusely from the body. The daughter vowed, saying, "If my filial piety is sincere, may this foul stench not arise.
As soon as she finished speaking, the blood ceased. Later, her father took a second wife, and they together cultivated the practice of Pure Land.

When the time of death approached, she requested a monk to explain the visualization methods of the Pure Land. Suddenly, she asked for her robes, lay down in a dignified manner, and grasped the hand of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Holding a banner, she passed away in silence. (From the *Wǎngshēng jí*).
Zheng Shi of the Song dynasty was a native of Qiantang. She daily recited the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* and never ceased her practice of Buddha-remembrance. Later, while ill, she requested a bath.
Having finished his bath, he sat facing west and asked his family members, "Do you hear the sound of the *ghaṇṭā*? The sages of the Pure Land are arriving.

Shortly thereafter, with palms joined, he leaped for joy and said, "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have come! Avalokiteśvara holds a golden platform in his hand, and the Tathāgata receives me to ascend it.
Thereupon, he passed away peacefully. (From the *Wǎngshēng jí*)
An envoy from Japan arrived to pay tribute during the Song dynasty. Their ship anchored in Putuo Bay, where they witnessed the miraculous manifestations of Avalokiteśvara.

Desiring to carry these relics back to their own country, they encountered a great storm as they prepared to depart; iron lotus flowers appeared across the entire bay, preventing the ship from moving forward.

Terrified, the Japanese returned them, and thus the place was named Lotus Harbor (Lianhua Gang). Furthermore, Wang Gui and others of the Imperial Household, acting on imperial decree, brought and presented ornate banners and precious incense.
They went to the mountain. In their hearts, they secretly doubted, saying, "In the midst of this vast expanse of water, where can the Bodhisattva be?
This is all merely people’s own deluded faith. Just as they were unmooring, iron lotus flowers filled the sea, and the wind and waves surged so violently that the boat could not move.

The people on board looked toward the mountain, wailing and prostrating themselves. When the wind and waves subsided slightly, there appeared a white ox floating across the mountain; it was entirely [visible].
They ate its blossoms, and only then could the boat be moved. Shortly thereafter, the ox returned to the water’s edge and transformed into a single white stone, which remains there to this day;
thus, Lianhua Yang (Lotus Flower Bay) is also called Shiniu Gang (Ox Stone Harbor).

In the thirteenth year of the Zhizhi era of the Yuan dynasty, when Chancellor Bayan pacified the region south of the Yangtze, the regional commander Halidai came to visit the entrance of Chaoyin Cave. Finding it was profoundly dark and nothing could be seen, he then spread...
He drew his bow and released an arrow, which pierced through [the vessel] and vanished. When they boarded the ship, iron lotuses sprang up again across the expanse of the ocean.

Consequently, they were struck with great terror; leading the multitude, they prostrated themselves in rows to repent and apologize. Suddenly, they beheld the Great Being clad in white robes, together with the image of a youth, manifesting upon the clouds.
Since the beginning of the Hongwu era of the Ming dynasty, those who have crossed the sea have become few, and such miraculous manifestations have been rarely seen. Nevertheless, Master Tang—
The boat reached Shenjiamen, where a golden alms bowl was still seen floating on the water.
On the nineteenth day of the tenth month in the twenty-first year of the Yongle era, the White-Robed Bodhisattva appeared at Chaoyindong, accompanied by dragon kings and dragon maidens.

At the hours of the Dragon (7–9 a.m. and the Snake (9–11 a.m.), he manifested with wide-open eyes and a face bearing signs of affliction. At the hour of the Horse (11 a.m.–1 p.m.), he manifested a purple body and faced a wall.
At the hour of the Rooster (5–7 p.m.), outside Sanchaeyan Rock, he manifested as a Bodhisattva in white robes and a golden crown, seated amidst a red sun.

On the night of the nineteenth day of the second month in the second year of the Zhengtong era, he manifested a precious jewel that emitted a great radiance. It is traditionally said that such divine responses were not limited to these instances.

During the Yuanping era, the monk Huigong of Pingjiang suffered from reversed stomach ailments and was unable to eat or drink. One night he dreamed that a cat entered his abdomen;
from then on, his illness grew increasingly severe, and he longed for fish. Huigong realized this was the retribution of his karma, so he resolved to recite the name of Bodhisattva Guanyin.)

He recited the mantra of Great Compassion one hundred and eight times every day. Later, he again dreamed that he had gone into the mountains and encountered a Daoist practitioner who said, "I shall give you medicine.
Suddenly, a youth dressed in green arrived before him carrying a chicken in a cage.
A cat leaped from the mouth of a monk and went straight into the cage to seize the chicken. He woke up with a start, and his illness was instantly cured. (From the *Baoying lu*)
In the fifth year of the Yuan Dade era, Zhang Pengshan, a scholar of the Jixian Academy, was commissioned by imperial decree to perform the ritual of *li-zhu*.
He went to Chaoyin Cave and beheld the form of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, appearing as if faintly upon the cave wall. Next, he proceeded to Shancai Cave, where the Youth suddenly manifested;
amidst auspicious clouds above his head, he again beheld the Great Being, adorned with a jeweled crown and necklaces, holding a willow branch, and protecting the Dharma.
Divine beings guarded and flanked her front. Zhang led his followers to pay their respects; after a long while, she gradually vanished. (From *Guanyin Ganying*).
In the second year of the Zhizhi era (*Yichou*, 1265), Wang Yu, over forty years of age and childless, lived in Daling Ward in Nanjing.
While at the home of his friend Mr. Ma, he saw the *White-Robed Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* before the household deity. He asked, "Where did this sūtra come from?

Ma replied, "In the spring of the Gengshen year, when the great army was returning south, they captured a person from the south and stayed overnight at my home. They left it behind as they departed, and I took it back.
I have recited it with single-minded devotion without slackening. On the night of the fourteenth day of the fourth month in the Dingmao year, his mother-in-law...
Lady Liu dreamed of a man dressed in white wearing a golden crown, who arrived carrying a young boy and said, "I have come with you to deliver this 'holy boy' (Shengnu).
Lady Liu received him in her arms, and she suddenly awoke. At the hour of Si (10–12 a.m. the following day, her wife Zhang gave birth to a son whose spirit and appearance were exceptionally refined;

He then made a vow to carve and distribute five hundred fascicles in order to repay the kindness of those who had carried them for him. In the Gengyin year of the Wanli era, Master Yuan Liaofan carved the *Qinsi Zhenquan* (The True Exposition on Seeking Heirs), which includes this scripture.

In the *Jì yàn* (Records of Miraculous Responses), there are frequent accounts of laypeople receiving the "double-wrapped garment" from the White-Robed One; such spiritual responses are numerous and cannot be recorded in full.
(From the *Báiyī jīng yàn*). Yuan Taoshi Shiliuniang was a native of Xuchun Village in Changshu. At the age of twenty-six, she became a widow and remained childless.

Wishing to be reborn in the Pure Land, she constantly recited the "Universal Gate Chapter" of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra. Suddenly, she dreamed of a person in white robes who held a white lotus in his hand.
She ate a single flower, and after she awoke, her mind and spirit were remarkably transformed. Subsequently, she constructed a small pavilion and faced west to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
After three years of reciting the Buddha’s name, she beheld the Buddha manifesting a brilliant light; upon the sutra case, there was a sphere of fire the size of a marble.
Fearing it would burn the scriptures, she struck it with her hand and obtained a single *śarīra* relic. At the time of her death, a transformation Buddha appeared.
He came to welcome [the scripture] and departed with the assembly.

(From the *Pure Land Verses on Good People*) On the twelfth day of the ninth month in the autumn of the fifteenth year of the Yongle era of the Ming Chengzu, an imperial decree was issued for the Buddhist scriptures to be conveyed to Dabeen Temple.
That night, the pagoda of the temple manifested the radiance of śarīra, like precious pearls. On the thirteenth day, they appeared in five colors.
A ray of light like a single hair-tip shone forth; auspicious clouds cradled the sun, and the wondrous forms of the thousand Buddhas, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and the Arhats all gathered together.
Subsequently, the Buddhist scriptures were issued and distributed as far as Huai’an. Furthermore, a five-colored circular halo was beheld, with variegated clouds filling the sky.
Within the clouds appeared Bodhisattvas, Arhats, celestial flowers, jeweled stupas, dragons, phoenixes, lions, and elephants. There were also red birds and white cranes wheeling in circles.
They circled [the palace] in flight. The ministers submitted a memorial to offer congratulations, and the Emperor was greatly delighted.
(From the *Huangming Tongji*) The Ming-dynasty physician-monk from Wenzhou, Fache (style name: Wuwang), was blind from childhood. He tried every means to cure his blindness without success;
he did nothing but recite the name of Avalokiteśvara day and night for fifteen years. One night, in a dream, he heard the Bodhisattva calling him and commanding him...

Previously, there was a man whose feet were bound by an object so that he could not move. The Bodhisattva sighed and said, "In your previous life, you were a moxibustion practitioner who mistakenly damaged people's eyes;
you must now undergo this retribution. Out of compassion for your sincere heart, I shall ensure that your food and clothing are abundant.

He then reached into his robe, took a handful of precious jewels, and gave them to him. Upon waking, the man’s medical practice flourished greatly, and his robes and alms bowl were provided in abundance.
He was extremely wealthy and later lived to a great age. (From "The Physician’s Exhortation in the Dark World" from the Tang Dynasty.
In the Wuyin year of the Chongzhen era of the Ming dynasty, a monk named Chuiji traveled north from Yangzhou. While passing through Xuyan on his way, he happened to suffer from pain in his ribs.
The four types of physicians could not cure him. He cried out in distress from one person to another and did not eat or drink for over thirty days.
One night, a friend said to him, "In your daily lectures on the sutras and śāstras, you always encouraged others to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara, saying it can save them from suffering.
Now that you are afflicted by this grave illness, why do you not take refuge in the Great Compassionate One to seek deliverance for yourself? At that time, his mind was clouded and confused.
In the meantime, upon hearing these words, he attained realization. He hurriedly ordered incense and candles to be prepared and chanted the name of Avalokiteśvara at a loud voice without ceasing.

By the fourth watch, his voice suddenly fell silent. The assembly was startled, believing him to have passed away. When they opened the door to look, he was sleeping soundly with his hair-knot intact.
In the afternoon, he suddenly called out, "I am extremely hungry. Prepare a meal for me quickly. Once he had finished eating, he was immediately able to rise and walk.
The assembly asked in astonishment, "By what cause did you recover? Huiji replied, "When I first uttered my name, the pain was like being cut with a knife.
After a long while, auspicious clouds suddenly appeared in the sky, and I saw Avalokiteśvara pouring ambrosia from a flask onto the crown of my head; its coolness permeated my very bones."

Sweat flowed like water, and he subsequently fell into a deep sleep; upon waking, he was completely restored. The assembly all joined their palms in praise, saying that the Bodhisattva’s response should indeed be thus.
Ming: Wu Zhang of Wujiang County lost his father at the age of eleven. His mother was Lady Lu. In the *Guimao* year of the Yongle era, she, as a widow—

aboard the boat, he installed an image of Avalokiteśvara and prayed with grief day and night, vowing that he must see his mother.

He was appointed to Raozhou in Jiangyou. While traveling across the sandy deserts, both his feet were cracked open. Lying in the corridor of a wilderness temple, he encountered a man of the Way named Jiao, who applied medicinal ointment and healed them.

Later, while seeking lodging in a solitary village, a woman requested that he share her bed; however, Chang— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "璋," which appears to be the beginning of a proper name, likely referring to the monk Daochang.)
He said, "I am like a half-dead, withered vine; how could there be any spring in me? He resisted [the monk] with all his might. When he went out the door, the snow was several feet deep.

Crawling forward on his hands and knees, he found an ancient temple where he could rest. There he saw the monk from before, who comforted him, saying, "For the sake of your mother, you have forgotten your own body."
He was truly a man of iron. Heaven did not fail his diligent efforts; he would soon see his mother. He brought out the cakes to eat them, and at dawn, he set out on the road.
Upon reaching Ráo, he sought out the Prince’s residence. His mother was indeed there. Zhāng repeatedly petitioned for permission to take her in for lifelong support.

His request was not granted. He then rented a room to the east of the prefectural office. On the wall, he inscribed the two large characters "Sishen" (Seeking One's Parents) and added a note beside them:
"Seeking my parents ten thousand *li* away, I have passed through a hundred hardships without regret; once I behold my mother, I swear that even nine deaths shall not deter me.

During the Zheng, Jia, and Jiajing eras, there was a man from Duanan named Zhou Tingzhang, whose courtesy name was Yuyu. By nature he was simple and honest;

"I do not depart from daily life, nor do I engage in craving or attachment; I hope only to be thus.

(From the *Jingang Lingying*). Ming Dynasty: Liu Guxian, a native of Huangzhou, was enlisted in the Left Tiger Guard Army. He once accompanied Grand Supervisor Zheng He on an embassy.

Everyone marveled at this. Liu said, "This fish carried me here; it nearly capsized several times, yet the fish would repeatedly lift us up with its fins and gills, so that water did not enter the boat.
A person on board asked, "What good deeds have you performed in your life?"
As a result, he obtained this retribution. Liu said, "He simply recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra. (From *Shanyutang Bisheng*).
At Nantai Temple in Fuzhou during the Ming dynasty, there was a statue of Avalokiteśvara that was about to be dismantled. A sculptor named Elder Lin requested permission to return and serve it.
Several months later, while navigating a boat into the sea, his vessel was wrecked and he was drowning. He urgently called out to Avalokiteśvara, saying, "I have always..."
"O Savior Bodhisattva! Why would the Bodhisattva not save me? Having finished speaking, his body spontaneously began to float. He obtained a board and mounted it;
