He returned with some resources, which people attributed to the assistance of Avalokiteśvara (*Guanyin*).

(From the *Bisheng*) Ming Dynasty’s Shen Jianquan went on a pilgrimage to Luochong Temple in Lili. Seeing that the rear hall was dilapidated, he observed that the head of the Avalokiteśvara statue was wearing a bamboo hat.
He sighed and said, "The Bodhisattva is compassionate and can bestow wisdom upon others. I vow to renovate this hall. He then sought...
"I have one or two descendants who study; that is sufficient. He returned home to consult his wife, and she said, "We currently have several hundred *shí* of rice.
It would be well to quickly exchange it for silver; with this alone, we can complete this meritorious deed. Before long, the buildings and the sacred image were finished.

It was brilliantly renewed. His grandson Yaozhong and his great-grandson Mengdou successively passed the imperial examinations (*Chūbiānxīnlù*). Wang Yingji of the Ming dynasty was long devoted to the worship of Avalokiteśvara.

In the *Ren-yin* year of the Wanli era, while returning to his hometown on a detour from an official mission to the East, he suffered from a phlegm-and-fire illness for seven days, unable to swallow even water or gruel. He dreamed that he was riding in a palanquin along the Great... [text continues].
By the riverbank, the man before him suddenly lost his footing, and the King tumbled into the water. Various kinds of scaly creatures appeared before him;
he thought to himself, "I have often eaten these creatures, yet now they present me with a peril.

In a daze, as if someone had lifted him up onto the cliff, he found the crimson sun high in the sky and the Great Being Avalokiteśvara sitting by the rock. The King reached out his hand and felt his robe.
He was not wet. He bowed in gratitude, and the Great Being said to him, "Your family has honored me for generations;

therefore, I have come to save you. However, because your karmic burden of killing is considerable, this illness has arisen. If you refrain from killing, you will recover. The King said, "To receive your compassionate power and be universally saved is my long-held aspiration.
How could I dare not obey your command? Suddenly he awoke, his body dripping with sweat like rain. From then on, he vowed his heart to the practice.
Abstaining from Killing. He himself composed the "Discourse on the Spirit of Abstaining from Killing" to record these matters (from the *Guangren pin*).
Ming Tai Wang Li-gu, courtesy name Bo-wu, passed the provincial examination in the Bingwu year of the Wanli era.

He dreamed of his father, the Grand Councilor Shi-xing, who instructed him that he would face five deaths over ten years and advised him to cultivate virtue to avert calamity. This occurred during the Jia... [year].
Before the Three Jewels, he vowed to observe a lifelong fast and received the four precepts against killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying according to the Tiantai school.
Later, while serving as the magistrate of Xingan County in Jiangxi, he completely abandoned these practices. In the year Wu-wu, he entered the capital for an audience.

While his boat was moored at Digang, he was summoned by the underworld at night. The presiding official shouted fiercely, saying: "Your allotted lifespan in the world of the living ended in the eighth month of Bing-chen; that you have been extended until now..."
"This is the power of fasting and purification. How can you abandon it? He ordered the register to be brought so that [the man] could see it;

he saw that beneath his name, the years and months were all annotated, until the eighth month of the *bingchen* year, when the space suddenly became blank. After Gu finished reading it, he prostrated himself and said, "In holding office, one cannot help but act this way.
The presiding official said, "What then, when your allotted lifespan is exhausted? He ordered him to be driven into prison. As he sat there, a subordinate official pleaded for him, saying:
He attempted to verify this by examining the matters following his breaking of the precepts. In a short while, two baskets arrived at his shoulders. He ordered them all to be opened;

there were the scrolls of Gan’s writings, as well as the occasional notes he had made in his daily life, down to every scrap of paper—all were present. From each, vapors rose upward, appearing in various colors—blue, white, red, and black—not of a single hue.
The master ordered each of them to search for it. First, they searched among the black and blue fragments, which formed a heap; next, they searched the white heap and the red heap.
By then, the blue fragments had gradually vanished, and the black ones had shrunk to the size of chopsticks, while the red ones remained brilliantly prominent and abundant.
Looking askance at the red heap beside the hub, he saw that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* he had engraved, along with the *Hao sheng bian* and the *She cang juan*, were all present within it.
The master said, "Even though you know to cultivate virtue, can you endure the loss of your five senses while preserving your life?
He then ordered his eyes to be gouged out. Immediately, he was blinded and could see nothing. He felt someone urging him away; with one stumble, he woke up.
Opening his eyes, he saw the lamp-light as if it were piercing needles, unable to open them at all. That night, he dreamed that someone again drove nails into his eyes, causing excruciating pain.

His blindness grew increasingly severe. He consequently withdrew from medical treatment and resolved to request retirement to return to his hometown. Abandoning his household life, he devoted himself to the cultivation of pure karma.
In the seventh month of the Gengshen year, while performing repentance rituals at Youxi, he dreamed one evening of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara sprinkling nectar with a willow branch upon his eyes.
Rising the next morning, his vision suddenly cleared; both eyes were restored to sight. Thereafter, he traveled extensively to Yunqi and Boshan.

Gate. Regarding true practice and authentic realization: the Reborn One (Saengjae) spent another twelve years [in training] and was titled Master Biru (Biryo Daesi). (From the *Record of Co-arising*).
During the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, the Minister of Revenue Lu Wutai of Pinghu had a servant who, while struggling with another person, mistakenly struck and injured him.
He was sentenced to death. Terrified, he sought refuge with the Duke, who said, "One who kills a person must face the laws of the state.
How could I possibly indulge my own feelings to seek your exoneration? While you are in prison, you should single-mindedly recite the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;
in three years, I shall come to pardon you. The man followed these instructions, maintaining his recitation without slackening at any time. After only one year, he encountered a general amnesty.

[The image] then emerged. (From the "Responses of Avalokiteśvara") Ming’s Xu Mingfu of Wu Commandery went to serve as an official in Chu and subsequently moved his family there. He was fond of learning and devoted to virtuous conduct, teaching his son to read.
He had long maintained a single scroll of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara and paid him profound reverence. His son’s name was Kuang; he was over ten years old.
Suddenly, he was stricken with a life-threatening illness. The husband and wife knelt before the Great Being (Mahāsattva) morning and evening, offering prayers.
On the seventh night, they dreamed that the Bodhisattva told them, "Do not grieve; your son shall rise again tomorrow morning. Suddenly, they heard a sound that shook the table.
Startled, they awoke and rose to look at the offerings before the Mahāsattva’s altar; the fruit platters and various vessels had all fallen to the ground, yet upon inspection, nothing was missing.
Regarding the first instance of his impairment: the son was mumbling in his mouth, calling out in a faint voice, "Bodhisattva, save me!

Bodhisattva, save me! When questioned, he did not respond. At dawn, [the father] inquired as to the reason. The son said, "Last night at the hour of midnight, while I was in a state of total delirium, I saw the Great Being arrive at the bedside.
He called to me, 'I shall save you,' and then, taking a bowl of water, commanded me to drink it. It was ice-cold."
A coolness permeated his very bones; consequently, his entire body broke into a sweat and he felt refreshed. Within a few days, his illness was indeed cured.
Later, his son Cheng became a jinshi in the *bingchen* year of the Wanli era. (From *Xu Shi Tingjun*).

During the Wanli period of the Ming dynasty, Jiao Jia served as a county clerk in Jiangyin. He was selected as a District Magistrate (*dianshi*) in Huguang and subsequently promoted to a Judicial Secretary (*zhishi*). He departed...
They traveled for three or four stages, mooring their boat upon the river. A monk from the south came along the Shu River seeking passage on their vessel.

The crew would not allow it, but the monk revealed his purpose to Jiao, saying: "I, a poor monk, have collected six hundred taels of gold with which I intend to go to Putuo to erect a banner and establish a temple for Avalokiteśvara.
I pray that you will let me travel south with you; this merit is truly immeasurable."
Jiao traveled with him for several days. Suddenly, an evil thought arose within him. One night during a great storm, he pushed the monk into the river.

He opened the monk’s chest and found, as expected, six hundred pieces of gold, which he took entirely into his private possession. When he rose at dawn, he saw the monk emerging from the water, advancing toward him to demand his life.
Jiao patted the monk on the back and said, "My life is at an end; however, this gold was bestowed by the people of the ten directions, and I shall certainly not give it to you."

It was so. From then on, he manifested his form day and night to cause disturbance. When [the official] rose from his seat at dawn, the monk was already by his side and said, "I have already petitioned the Emperor on your behalf.
The Emperor is enraged and intends to execute you and your son. [The official] became consumed with anxiety and fear, fell ill, and could find no peace whether sitting or lying down.
At every post station he reached, he invited monks and Daoists to perform rites for his deliverance; yet in the petitions, he did not dare to write the true reason directly, only—
He merely prostrated himself, earnestly entreating and repenting for his transgressions. He lingered and returned home, where his illness grew even more severe.

He vowed to use this gold to perform Buddhist rites, undertaking every possible ritual of expiation and thanksgiving; yet, when the time for the monk's arrival came, [the monk] would invariably shout out, "What benefit is there in these meritorious deeds?
Return my six hundred pieces of gold! I am going to the South Sea! Sometimes he would come from atop the roof, or sometimes he would emerge from within the walls.
At times he would sit upon his bed leaning against the screen; shortly thereafter, the family members all saw him and fled in alarm, crying out in unison, "The Master has come!

They entreated him with every means at their disposal, but the monk would never consent. After Jiao had been there for nearly a year, both the monk's belongings and his own provisions were almost entirely exhausted.
He languished in a state of misery, awaiting death. Suddenly one day, a deceased monk arrived bearing a visiting card; the gatekeeper declined to admit him, citing that the master was critically ill.
The monk rebuked him, saying, "I am no ordinary guest; I must see your master to save his remaining breath.
At that time, Jiao was prostrate upon his pillow groaning, while his wife and children wept all around him. They all beheld the monk’s form and further heard him announce his name outside.

Jiao, filled with bitter resentment, cried out, "The life-taking demon has manifested such transformations! It would be better to die quickly. He then threw himself beneath the bed and took up a knife, intending to commit suicide.
His family members struggled to hold him back, but the monk had already burst directly into the room.

Addressing Jiao, he said, "I am a human being, not a ghost. You must clear your wife and children from here so that I may tell you the truth. The family members then stepped aside to give way. The monk—
He said, "Last year, my wandering soul was tossed amidst wind and waves; I was certain to die. Suddenly, I saw Avalokiteśvara descend from the sky, holding a lamp and leading me into a reed island.
There I encountered fishermen who rescued me. Although these six hundred pieces of gold were taken by you for my sake,"
I have continued my fundraising until the required number was reached; I am now taking it to Putuo to fulfill this long-held vow.

Recently, while passing through Jiangyin, I heard that you were suffering from a strange illness, so I relied on that report to come and see you, merely to dispel your delusion regarding the "cup-snake.
Jiao said, "It is fortunate that you, Master, did not die, but since my gold is exhausted, how can I repay you? The monk laughed and said, "In coming here, I did not seek anything at all."

Jin Jiao and his entire family were moved by gratitude and prostrated themselves in worship. They wished to provide him with clothing and footwear as gifts, but he firmly declined and would not accept them;

having partaken of but a single meal, he departed. When people followed his tracks, they found that he had indeed boarded a sea vessel and gone away. From that time on, his ghostly form was seen no more.
However, his ailment was never cured, and he passed away after several months. He had only one son, who possessed literary talent from a young age.
Just as he was about to take the imperial examinations, he was unable to go because of his father’s death. While walking by the river, he suddenly leapt into the waves and drowned.
When the monk returned from the South Sea, he heard of this and sighed for a long time. (From the *Induced Responses Section with Additions*)
In the Jiayin year of the Wanli era, Wu Yide of Shixian followed his uncle Zhengkun to receive instruction at Lindang Temple.

When Zhengkun consulted with Master Pumen and attained realization, he subsequently took refuge in the Buddha-dharma; moreover, in his later years, he led his disciples in observing the fast and prostrating toward the Western Pure Land.
Yide was particularly profound in his reverent faith, vowing to transcribe fifty fascicles of the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Thirty fascicles. On the twenty-ninth day of the fifth month, while bathing at Qin Stream, he suddenly fell ill and lost consciousness.

He was carried back and laid as a corpse upon his bed. Suddenly he spoke, saying: "I am Guan, the left-hand Dharma-protector before the Buddha. Because Yi De mistakenly killed me, I was seized by my karmic resentment and brought into the underworld.
However, because he serves the Buddha and maintains virtuous thoughts regarding the scriptures, I have come specifically to protect him. Kun, you should recite [the scriptures] for him."
The Buddha recited a sutra and waited for the seventh day, when Yi-de would return to life, so that he might transcribe the scripture to fulfill his vow;
by means of this merit, the resentful ghost could attain deliverance. On the seventh day, Yi-de indeed revived. Supporting himself on his waist, he cried out repeatedly in pain from his fall.
When his uncle asked the reason, he told him: "While bathing in the stream, I saw two men coming toward me holding a tablet and calling my name. I followed them, thinking all the while of my family."

It was of no avail to seek rescue; it would have been better for me to have recited the Buddha’s name on my own. In a brief moment, I entered a city and saw from afar a signboard inscribed with the words “The Hall of the Forest of Luminaries” (Senra-dien).
To the left were the offices of the Four Births, and to the right were the offices of the Four Deaths. Lord Yan sat upon the dais, surrounded by countless head-holding demons.
Upon my arrival, I rushed forward and struck out at them. A man wearing a black cap sitting to the side asked, “What are you saying? I stumbled [in response].

With no place to set foot, he could only silently recite the Buddha’s name. When he was flogged and beaten, he realized that the pain could be endured through mindfulness of the Buddha; yet in the end, he remained dazed and unconscious.
The judge led him to a clear-water pool to wash his chest, where he saw his own five viscera. Only then did he realize that in his previous life he had been a general.
"I have mistakenly killed eight hundred lives. Now that my karma is full and I am receiving this rebirth, they demand retribution and will not let me go;

On the fifth day of the fifth month, he passed by a tavern on his way home and saw one of his servants holding a brocade robe while presiding over a lawsuit involving a man's life, wielding all manner of influence. When a single word did not suit his purpose, the servant tore the robe to shreds.

The students responded with "Yes, yes," and received his instructions. That night, his wife dreamed that the Great Being (Bodhisattva) said to her:

Ming Dynasty filial son Peng Youyuan, courtesy name Xinyu, was a native of Yiyang, Huguang. From childhood, he recited the Mahāsattva [Avalokiteśvara] with devotion.

He then bathed his body and prostrated himself. Raising his hands to touch his heart, he sought out the location of his lungs and liver. Taking a knife, he pierced himself; with the first incision, blood gushed forth;

By the sixth incision, the heart emerged; following the heart, he reached the lungs, and following the lungs, he reached the liver. At that moment, the pain was such that he nearly died. After a short while, it subsided slightly.
He revived. His wife was then summoned and ordered to quickly boil the liver to serve to his mother. The mother, unaware of what had happened, joyfully took a bite.

Her illness was immediately cured as if by magic. When the news spread, people near and far offered praise. Observing that his lungs protruded prominently from his chest and the wound had not yet closed, the multitude prayed to the gods.
The Great Being appeared in a dream and said: "These are the lungs of a filial son; there is no difficulty in recovering them."

In this degenerate age, those who possess benevolence and filial piety are rare. [The author] wished to display [this child] for one hundred days so that the people of the world might behold him everywhere.

At that time, the lady had only recently become pregnant, and she indeed gave birth to a son.
In the *xinsi* year of the Chongzhen era of the Ming dynasty, a man from Shandong who was paralyzed from the waist down arrived at Dangtu County.

...of suffering. Gu said, "If you can resolve to leave the household life, relying on the great power of compassion, there may be a donor who will assist you.

The man with the paralysis followed him, whereupon he shaved his head and received the precepts of purity. Although he went begging for alms, he did not consume meat or blood; and though he was subjected to insults and abuse, [he remained steadfast].
He accepted this with patience. Gu further instructed him to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara and to maintain the Cundī-dhāraṇī.
After he had practiced these for over two years, in the autumn of the Wuzi year, he suddenly dreamed one night that an old woman called out to him, saying, "Arise! Arise!"
The paralyzed man said, "I am a cripple; how could I possibly rise? The old woman took hold of both his feet with her hands and straightened them, so that they were no longer contracted.
When he rose in the morning, his paralysis had vanished, and he was once again a dignified and imposing monk.
He took the name Ban Ya (Half-Crag), and thereupon people began to offer him sustenance. (From Tang Yizhi’s *Ji qi shu*).
During the Hongwu era of the Ming dynasty, Long Zihui of Luling County in Jizhou and his wife, Lady Xiao, were deeply devoted to one another as husband and wife.
Yet, they found it extremely difficult to obtain an heir. In the tenth month of the year Jimao, his younger sister Shurou obtained a copy of the *Heart Sūtra* with five seals on white silk.

He made a vow to observe the fasts and recite the sutras, and further pledged to bestow one thousand scrolls of scripture upon laypeople.

On the sixteenth day of the eighth month of the following year, he gave birth to a son whose appearance was refined and elegant; he was named Guisheng (Jasmine-Born). Thus, it truly accorded with his prayers. Furthermore, in the fourth year of the Xuande era...
Zhang Gui of Zhangde Prefecture accompanied the Prince of Huai to his fiefdom in Guangdong, where he obtained the *Baiyi jing* (Sutra of the White-Robed One).
After six years, he returned to his hometown and, together with his wife, Lady Tian, resolved to offer the sutra as a vow to seek offspring. Before long, they had a son;

One hundred fascicles. In the second month of the Ding-si year, she again gave birth to a son. The evidence of these manifestations was as clear and manifest as this (from the *Baiyi jingji yan*).
Ming’s Liu Daolong’s mother, Lady Li, was forty years old; she observed the long fast and served the Buddha, though she did not understand how to recite the scriptures.

He did not cease his efforts even in winter. He carved and distributed copies of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and he encouraged others to receive, recite, and make offerings to them, exhausting his resources without regard for his own means.

He continued in this manner for twenty-five years. One year before his death, he drew out the surplus funds from his textile workshops and invited renowned monks to chant the sutras, performing great meritorious deeds.
When these affairs were concluded, he dreamed at night that the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara) whom he had venerated appeared to him, holding a string of white beads and showing it to him.
He said, "I give this to you; the number of these pearls is the time for your rebirth in the Pure Land.

She counted them in her dream and found there were fifty-three beads, yet she did not understand their meaning. On the thirteenth day of the fifth month of the Gengzi year, she suddenly told her family members, "I am departing today.
You must all recite the Buddha’s name aloud together to assist me in going to the West. Her son’s wife—
The group sat together before the platform, chanting the Buddha’s name in unison. After some time, they passed away while sitting upright facing west (*Kongjanglingying*).
Zhu Dezhen of the Ming dynasty was a native of Jiangling; she was the third daughter of the Prince of Yi, Chang Mang. Her grandfather was Zhuyong. There is... [text fragment].

Xianming once compiled the *Shan neixun* (Good Inner Training) of Empress Renxiao, the *Nüxun* (Instructions for Women) of Empress Dowager Zhangsheng, the *Gulie nüzhuanchuan* (Biographies of Ancient Exemplary Women), the *Nüxiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety for Women), and the *Nüjie* (Admonitions for Women).
These works formed the *Nüjiao daceng* (Great Achievement of Female Education), which was circulated throughout the world. When the girl was young, she received virtuous instruction at home.

When Zhongxian died prematurely at the age of ten, she heard the news of his passing and immediately abstained from meat and donned white mourning garments. She further vowed, "I shall by no means become a widow; I will rather die. Thereupon she ceased eating and hanged herself. Her parents were struck with terror and no longer discussed the matter of marriage. (The year was) Tianqi Xinyou.

In the eighth month of autumn, arriving at the anniversary of the death of Zhongxian, he first paid his respects to his parents and took leave of the ancestral temple. On the twenty-ninth day of the eighth month, he returned to the palace.

Wearing plain mourning bands and holding a staff, he performed the rites of wailing and presented offerings. He composed the following text himself for the sacrifice to Zhongxian: "Lord Gong died young, and Lady Gong remained steadfast in her virtue;
until death she would not think of another. Her resolve was like that of the *Bozhou* (The Cypress Boat). Through the ages, fortunes rise and fall, yet the heart remains constant."

There is no distinction between past and present. Alas for this widowed woman! Born into the imperial clan, she was betrothed at the age of eight; her destined partner was truly fixed. How could such misfortune have befallen her? Her husband suddenly passed away in childhood.
Though she is but young, she reflects silently upon the fundamental principles of human relations. Her ancestors and the King were lovers of the worthy, and her parents delighted in goodness.

She has long been familiar with the *Nai Ze* (Instructions for the Inner Quarters), having observed their fragrant regulations through practice. Within the palace gates, she shall wear coarse white silk forever, renouncing all rouge and powder. Firmly...
I maintain my integrity and filial piety to bring glory to our state. Now that I have reached the age of maturity (*jī*), I shall resolve to die rather than yield.

I call upon Heaven and knock at the palace gates, hoping that the Censors will take heed; I swear not to remarry, but to follow one man until death. All say this is most fitting, which somewhat eases my anxious heart. I ascend to your hall and establish your seat;
I shed these tears from my blood and pour forth this blood-stained lament. I am willing to uphold the way of a wife and serve you.
"My maternal uncle and my father-in-law shall one day share the same grave; will I not feel ashamed?

She petitioned the authorities for recognition of her conduct, but as she had not yet reached the required age, they cited the precedent of Lady Long of the Huai Province to grant her an annual allowance of fifty *shí* of rice. She subsequently cleared and purified a chamber for her practice.
I take refuge in the Triple Gem. In the morning, I recite the Universal Gate Chapter and the Great Compassion Mantra; in the evening, I recite the Amitābha Sūtra and the Rebirth Mantra.

I vow never again to compose any poems or prose. On the birthdays of my elders and parents, as well as on the anniversaries of their deaths, I shall invariably prepare offerings and perform repentance rites from dawn until nightfall, following the ritual protocols without error.
When the bhikṣuṇīs and the laywomen who maintain the fast hear of this, they will rejoice.

Whenever anyone sought an audience with her, she strictly forbade it. Once a female servant reached the age of thirteen, she was immediately dismissed. Her parents-in-law also devoted their hearts to the vegetarian diet; all fruits and delicacies were personally prepared by her before being served.
She was invariably diligent when attending to the sick or inquiring after their well-being. In the year of Jiǎzǐ, her father fell gravely ill.

She cut flesh from her own thigh to offer him, and that night her father dreamed of the Great Being (Bodhisattva), who said: "Because of your filial devotion as a daughter, your father’s life shall be prolonged and his illness cured."
He was cured. There was no one among the people of Jianggan who did not praise his integrity and filial piety (*Qiqing Yesheng*).

There he met an extraordinary monk, who cautioned him, saying: "You will face great peril; if you can maintain the recitation of the name of the Holy One of Great Compassion, it may be averted. The Master vowed [to do so].

Seeing that warhorses were swarming everywhere, he traveled east to Kunshan, where he preached the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Golden Light Sūtra* in a pure chamber.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and other scriptures were revered by both monastics and laypeople. On the second day of the first month of the Renchen year, he sat upright and preached a verse to pass away (*from the *Fahua Gantong Lu*).
Cheng Boli, a prominent merchant of the Qing dynasty who resided in Yangzhou for a long time, served Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva with great devotion. In the Yiyu year...
In the summer, as the army passed by Yangcheng, Cheng prayed to the Great Being (Mahāsattva) for deliverance.

In a dream, the Great Being said to him, "Seventeen people in your household—sixteen members in total—shall all be spared. Only you are among those whose lives cannot be saved. Upon waking, Cheng again offered earnest prayers.

He ordered sixteen members of his household to stay in the eastern wing, while he himself remained in the central hall to await them, lest he bring trouble upon his family.
Cheng Xin kept his word. Five days later, the soldiers arrived at the gate. Cheng went out to meet them and asked, "Are you Wang Mazǐ?
I owe you twenty-six blows; you may kill me, for otherwise I have no enmity toward you. The soldiers—

He then struck Cheng twenty-six times with the back of his blade and then released him. (Recorded by Tang Yizhi)
He said: "There are three intentions in recording this matter. First, it shows that the great compassion of a Bodhisattva can transform fixed karma.
Second, it shows that once past karma has matured, it is difficult to escape its consequences; from now on, one must be careful not to create new karma for the future.
Third, it shows that all that is currently experienced is entirely due to past causes; one should accept this with joy and not [resist it]."
Do not harbor resentment; nor is it necessary to strive with great hardship to avoid a distracted mind. It is further said:
"Those who reverently serve Avalokiteśvara will surely possess deep faith in cause and effect. Throughout their lives, their good deeds will surely be many and their evil deeds few;
their wholesome thoughts will surely be many and their unwholesome thoughts few. Because this body and mind do not form conditions with evil, [the retribution for evil] may be avoided."
This is no mere coincidence. (From the *Yi-ji-qiu-shu*):
The family of Yu Shu of Jintan in the Great Qing dynasty was characterized by filial piety and loyalty. The entire household followed the Buddha;

In the winter of the Dingyou year, he was arrested and taken to Jiangning due to the false accusations of his enemies; there was no one near or far who did not feel pity for him.

Thus, he finally attained exoneration. Shanxiu was profoundly filial; every night he would pray to the Northern Dipper naked for his father’s sake.

He did not cease even in the bitter cold, continuing until the matter was resolved. Had there been no reliance upon the Buddha-dharma, Shanxiu alone would have been sufficient to demonstrate filial devotion unto death, let alone those such as Shuyan.

Lady Shiuan also maintained the Cundi fast. Every morning she knelt devoutly and recited the sutras. Before long, her chronic ailments were entirely cured.

In the Great Qing, at Mount Huangtu in Moling, the mother of Liu [Surname] was forty-eight years old when she sought a son and obtained one, who emerged from her womb.

In the year Jichou (609), when Liu was twenty-nine and his younger brother nineteen, they set out together for the South Sea.

Regarding the power of Avalokiteśvara to rescue and deliver, Tang Yizhi said: "On the fifteenth day of the third month in the year of Gengyin, Liu Yue and Monk Ding came to visit me.
On that day, we were performing a rite for releasing living beings (*fangsheng*). An elder was staying at my lodging, and Monk Ding took his leave of him.
To this day, I remain dissatisfied with this. Alas! When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rescues people from suffering and distress, it does not necessarily have to be upon the sea."
Furthermore, such instances are especially frequent at sea. Yet, while the distance is over two thousand *li*, one arrives home in an instant;
and upon entering the water, one’s clothes remain dry—of this, we have simply not heard before. (From the *Jiqiu shu*).
Yang Huang, style name Xizhou, of Daqing, was a native of Dangtu. His family had resided for generations at Lishu Fen in Guanyu and were devoted to the study of Confucianism.
As he was traveling, the local records were strange and erroneous; following the established precedents of the law, he became trapped and delayed there. Just then, troops surrounded his hometown.

Huang hurriedly rushed into the water and died. His son was only ten years old; seeing his father drown from among the trees, he too wailed and ran to throw himself into the water.
On the sixteenth day of the third month of the *pingxu* year of the Shunzhi era, after three hours had passed, the two corpses emerged floating together, embracing one another.

Those who saw him shed tears. His wife, Lady Lu, lamented that her husband would have no progeny; she vowed to abstain from meat and blood and enshrined a Buddha image in their home, weeping bitterly morning and night as she recited the Buddha’s name.
Suddenly, one night, she dreamed of an old woman carrying a son who said, "I leave this child to you.
Upon waking, she sighed and said, "I pray that my husband Zhang may have a son born of his widow womb; this would be a gift from the Bodhisattva. At the end of the year, she gave birth to a daughter.

Lady Lu wept and said, "It is all over. In the spring of the Dinghai year, she assembled the elders of the clan and announced, "Since I have no son, my meager fields should be divided among my nephews;
I shall have enough to provide for our basic food and clothing so that I may care for this girl. Having spoken, she wept again.

The clan elders could not bear it and said, "Wait until the first anniversary of her death (xiaoxiang), and we will perform Buddhist rites for Huang and then discuss the division of the property. When the time arrived, they prepared a gathering for the relatives and distributed [the inheritance].

On the evening of the fast, which was also the sixteenth day of the third month, the daughter wept incessantly. Her handmaid took her onto the pillow, where she lay as if in a nightmare, dazed and unconscious.

The daughter’s strange crying grew even more intense. The mistress called out loudly until she finally regained consciousness; when she took the girl into her arms, the girl was no longer in her female form.
Lu was greatly alarmed, and the family members all went to see her. They saw that her face and features remained exactly as before, yet she was private—[meaning she had become a man].

A male organ grew from his side, and there were still traces of blood nearby. The multitude was all struck with wonder; they finally realized that the Bodhisattva’s spiritual presence was real and that their previous dream had not been false.
They vied with one another to come before the Buddha and prostrate themselves, renaming him Fuci (Buddha-given). The following day, spectators crowded the gate.
When County Magistrate Zhang took the child into the courtyard to inspect him, he was still not convinced. He inquired about the child’s lineage, and everyone spoke with one voice in agreement.
The words said: "If the transformation of the child is not real, why do you nephews not wish to divide the fields and houses? The Marquis then ceased to doubt it.
How extraordinary! The day the Buddha bestowed the transformed body was the very day the father and son met their deaths.

Yet, were it not for Huang’s upright integrity in life, the son’s supreme filial piety in sacrificing himself for his father, and the wife’s wailing that moved Heaven, how could such a thousandfold encounter have occurred?
Is this not a rare occurrence seen only once in a hundred years? I have a further observation:
if it were merely a transformation granted by the Buddha, who else could believe it when it was not during a gathering of kinsmen? (From Tang Yizhi’s *Ji qi qiu shu*).

The Great Compassionate Heart Dharani of Avalokiteśvara,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra of the Great Tang.
I prostrate to Avalokiteśvara, Lord of Great Compassion, whose body of marks and signs is profound through the power of his vows.
Adorned with a thousand arms, you universally protect and sustain; With the radiance of a thousand eyes, you observe and illuminate all.
Proclaiming secret mantras from within words of truth, You give rise to compassion from within the unconditioned mind.
Swiftly fulfill all hopes and aspirations, And forever cause all sinful karma to be extinguished.
May the assembly of dragons, devas, and holy ones protect us with compassion; May we suddenly cultivate and refine hundreds of thousands of samādhis.
The body that upholds [this dharma] is a banner of radiant light; The mind that upholds it is a treasury of supernormal powers.
Washing away the dust and toil of worldly afflictions, may we vow to cross the ocean [of suffering]; May this be the gateway of skillful means for attaining supreme enlightenment.
I now recite this vow of refuge, May all my aspirations be fulfilled according to my heart’s desire.
Namo to the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara! May I swiftly come to know all dharmas.
Namo to the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara! May I early attain the eye of wisdom.
Homage to the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara; May I swiftly deliver all sentient beings.
Homage to the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara; May I soon attain skillful means.
Homage to the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara; May I swiftly board the ship of Prajñā.
Homage to the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara; may I quickly cross the sea of suffering.
Homage to the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara; may I swiftly attain the path of precepts and meditative concentration.
Homage to the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara; may I soon ascend the mountain of nirvāṇa.
Homage to the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara; May I quickly reach the abode of the unconditioned.
Homage to the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara; May I soon become one with the Dharma-nature body.
If I should approach the mountain of blades, The mountain of blades shall spontaneously crumble; If I should approach the cauldrons of fire, The cauldrons of fire shall spontaneously dry up.
The boiling water shall extinguish itself; If I am headed for hell, hell shall dry up of its own accord;
If I am headed for the realm of hungry ghosts, the hungry ghosts shall be spontaneously satiated;
If I am headed for the asuras, their evil minds shall be naturally subdued; If I am headed for the animal realm, I shall naturally attain great wisdom.
Having made this vow, one should with a sincere heart invoke my name and also single-mindedly recollect my original teacher, Amitābha Tathāgata.

Thereafter, one should immediately chant this divine dhāraṇī mantra. If one completes five full recitations over the course of a single night, the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas within one's body shall be extinguished.
Homage to the Tathāgata Amitābha.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if there are humans or devas who recite and uphold this Great Compassion Dhāraṇī..."
Regarding the "phrase": at the time of death, the Buddhas of the ten directions will all come to offer their hands.
Whichever Buddha-land one wishes to be born in, one shall attain rebirth there in accordance with that vow. Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, if any sentient beings who recite and uphold this Great Compassionate Divine Mantra should fall into the three evil realms, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment. [May this be true for] those who recite and uphold the Great Compassionate Divine Mantra."
If I do not give birth in the lands of all Buddhas, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.
If those who recite and uphold this Great Compassion Divine Mantra do not attain immeasurable samādhi and eloquence, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.
If those who recite and uphold this Great Compassionate Heart Mantra do not have all their requests fulfilled within their present lifetime, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.
It is named the *Mahākaruṇā-hṛdaya-dhāraṇī*. It excludes only those who are unwholesome and those who lack sincerity.

If there are women who loathe and despise their female bodies and desire to become men, should they recite and uphold the verses of this *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* and yet not transform their female bodies into male ones, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment. [If you] give rise to even a slight doubt...

Such a person will certainly not attain the fruition of their goal. If sentient beings encroach upon or damage the food, drink, or property belonging to the Sangha (the permanent residence), they cannot be absolved through repentance even during the appearance of a Buddha in the world;
even if they were able to repent, [the offense] would not be extinguished. Now, by reciting this Great Compassion Divine Mantra, it shall be immediately extinguished.
If one has encroached upon or consumed the food, drink, or property belonging to the Sangha, one must [repent] before the ten directions.

The Master repents and apologizes, and only then are they eliminated and extinguished. Now, when one recites the Mahākaruṇā Dhāraṇī, the Buddhas of the ten directions immediately come to act as witnesses;

all karmic obstacles and hindrances are completely eradicated. This includes all ten evil deeds, the five heinous crimes, slandering people, slandering the Dharma, breaking the fast, breaking the precepts, destroying stupas, ruining temples, stealing the property of the Saṃgha, and defiling the pure Brahma-conduct. Such [sins]...
All such evil karmas and grave offenses shall be completely extinguished, with one sole exception:

for those who harbor doubt regarding the mantra, even minor offenses and light karmas will not be extinguished, let alone grave offenses. Although these grave offenses may not be extinguished immediately, [they will eventually be so].
It can still serve as a distant cause for attaining Bodhi. Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, if any among gods or humans recite and uphold this Dharani of Great Compassionate Heart, they shall obtain fifteen kinds of auspicious births and avoid fifteen kinds of miserable deaths.
As for those miserable deaths: first, it shall not cause such a person to die from the suffering of hunger; second, it shall not lead them to die while imprisoned or shackled."
1. Death by flogging with a staff. 2. Death by being beaten with a cane. 3. Not dying as a victim of an enemy or adversary.
4. Not dying in the clash of military arrays. 5. Not dying from the predatory harm of tigers, wolves, or other fierce beasts. 6. Not dying from being stung by venomous snakes, vipers, or scorpions.
7. Not dying from fire or drowning in water. 8. Not dying from the effects of poisonous drugs.
9. They do not die from being harmed by *gū* (poisonous charms). 10. They do not die from insanity or loss of mindfulness. 11.
They do not die from falling from mountains, trees, cliffs, or precipices. 12. They do not die from the malevolent sorcery of wicked people. 13.
They do not die because malevolent spirits or evil ghosts find an opportunity against them. 14. They do not die from malignant diseases.
Fifteenth, one does not die by self-inflicted harm through improper means.
Those who recite and uphold the Great Compassionate Divine Mantra shall not suffer these fifteen kinds of evil deaths. They shall attain fifteen kinds of virtuous births:
first, wherever they are born, they will always encounter a benevolent king; second, they will always be born in a virtuous land; third, they will always meet with favorable times; fourth...
1. One constantly encounters virtuous friends. 2. The faculty of the body is always fully endowed. 3. The aspiration for the Path matures purely. 4.
One does not transgress the prohibitive precepts. 5. All one’s kinsmen and retinue are harmonious in their kindness and righteousness.
6. One’s requisites, wealth, and food are always abundant and sufficient. 7. One is constantly received with respect and assistance by others. 8. Whatever [one possesses]...
12. One’s wealth and treasures shall not be plundered by others. 13. Whatever one desires and seeks shall all be fulfilled accordingly. 14.
Dragon deities and benevolent spirits will constantly provide protection and guardianship. 15. In whatever place one is born, one shall see the Buddhas and hear the Dharma. 16.
Regarding the True Dharma one hears, one shall awaken to its most profound meaning. If one recites and upholds this Mahākaruṇā Dhāraṇī, [these benefits shall be obtained].
One shall attain these fifteen kinds of virtuous births. All devas and humans should constantly recite and uphold this, without giving rise to indolence.
After the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara had spoken these words, he stood with palms joined before the assembled multitude.

Toward all sentient beings, he gave rise to a heart of great compassion; with a smiling countenance, he then spoke these divine and wondrous verses of the Greatly Vast, Perfect, and Unobstructed Heart-Dhāraṇī of Great Compassion. The dhāraṇī says:

Kāluṇika-ye (this is the original body of Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; he holds a *paṭaha* drum and a *vajra*). Oṃ (all these spirits join their palms and listen as the mantra is recited).

Yakṣari (This is the Heaven of the Thirty-three. The celestial deity Maheśvara leads the heavenly armies; he is blue in color. Mahābodhisattva (This is the true mind;

The Buddha himself. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Master. Hūlu hūlu mara (these are the kings of the eight classes of ghost spirits).

*Buddhaya* (this is Ānanda’s former self), *Maitriya* (this is Bodhisattva Mahāratha, who holds a golden knife in his hand),

When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara had finished reciting this mantra, *svāhā*, the great earth shook in six ways, and the heavens rained down precious flowers that fell in profusion.
All the Buddhas of the ten directions were filled with joy, while the heavenly Māras and non-Buddhist heretics were struck with terror, their hair standing on end. I.
The entire assembly all attained the realization of the fruits: some attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, some the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, some the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and some the fruit of *arhat*.
Some attained the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and even up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
Immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta.
The *Sutra of the Heart Dhāraṇī of the Five Seals of the Great Compassionate One in White Robes*.
I prostrate to the Greatly Compassionate One, Vajradhara! Through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, you enter samādhi;
Your voice, like the surging tide of the ocean, responds to the human world. To all who have aspirations, You shall surely grant their wishes as they desire.

Homage to the Original Teacher Amitābha Buddha.

homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara in White Robes.
[I take refuge in] the front seal, the rear seal, and the seal for subduing demons; the heart seal, the body seal, and the dhāraṇī. I now recite this divine mantra.
I only pray that you will descend through your compassion and protect me (recite these eight characters three times).

*Kāya oṃ tārī tāri tud-tāri tud-tud-tāri svāhā.* (Hé-ā,
lā, dá, duō, jié, shǎo, duǒ, jí, zhuó. The Liturgy for Paying Homage to Avalokiteśvara.

Purifying the three karmas, with single-minded devotion, one prostrates with the five limbs touching the ground and takes refuge in Namo the Compassionate Father of the Ten Directions, the Vastly Miraculous and Responsive Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

Through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, one enters samādhi and attains the two types of compliance, the four inconceivables, the fourteen fearlessnesses, the nineteen methods of preaching the Dharma, the seven calamities and two supplications, and the thirty-two manifestations. Without...

Measuring your merit, you manifest great majestic power and give rise to great vows, flowing together with the nine realms and the six paths of four types of birth within the cycle of birth and death.
You employ hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of immeasurable *Ganges-sand* eons of skillful means and virtuous conduct to rescue and deliver all sentient beings without ceasing.
I now entreat you with compassion; please grant your grace and protection. I prostrate.

I reflect that [Name] has long been fortunate in past lives to have encountered the Buddha Vehicle. Although my body has left the household life, my mind has not been stained by the Way (*for a layperson:

though my body suffers amidst worldly conditions, my mind is largely distracted*). I am ignorant and hold false views; my faculties are clouded and obstructed. Furthermore, I fear that the power of my merit is shallow and my lifespan will not be long, such that I shall enter the Gate of Emptiness (*for a layperson:
such that I have merely obtained a human body*) in vain, living and dying in futility. Now, I wash my heart and weep with blood.
With bowed head and sincere devotion, throughout the day and all through the night, I contemplate the holy countenance, uphold the holy name, and prostrate before the holy image.

I pray only that the Bodhisattva’s celestial ear may hear my voice, that with a compassionate heart you may rescue me from suffering, and that out of pity you will bestow your protection by emitting great divine light.

It illuminates my body and mind, pouring down a great rain of nectar that drenches the crown of my head. It washes away the enmities and transgressions accumulated over successive lifetimes and cleanses the defilements of a thousand births.
My body and mind become pure, and demonic obstacles are eliminated. Whether sitting or lying down, throughout the day and night, [I remain thus].
Beholding the Bodhisattva emitting great divine light, may he open the nature of my wisdom, so that [I], at this very moment, may have my spiritual powers clearly manifest,
possess intelligence and sagacity, attain great eloquence, attain great wisdom, attain a long life, and attain great peace and happiness.
Practicing Chan and studying the Way, may you be free from all demonic obstacles; awakening to the patience of non-arising, may you practice the Bodhisattva path in life after life.

May you fully repay the four debts of gratitude and provide equal sustenance for those in the three realms of existence, so that all sentient beings throughout the Dharma realm may together perfect the Buddha-wisdom.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion, Vast and Miraculous Response (Recite three times and prostrate three times).
Regarding the three points on correcting errors, Master Lianchi said:
"As for the *Gao-wang Guanshiyin Jing*, it is traditionally said that Emperor Gao sang it and was thereby delivered from calamity. This...
This is an error. That scripture is vulgar and its composition lacks coherent meaning; it is unknown from which era it was translated.
Judging by reason, it is simply the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. People during the reign of Emperor Gao used this to escape calamities, and thus it was given that name.

Later generations did not know this and fabricated false words, calling it the *Gao Wang Jing* (Sutra of King Gao). Consequently, its name became confused with its meaning, and the laity remained unaware of this.

Furthermore, it is said that within the *Xiang Shan Juan* (Volume on Fragrant Mountain), it is claimed that Avalokiteśvara was the daughter of King Miaozhuangwang, who left home to attain the Way and was thus named Avalokiteśvara.
This is an error. Avalokiteśvara is an ancient Buddha of the past; through the thirty-two transformations, he delivers sentient beings by assuming forms according to their kind. Or...
She merely manifested in a female body; it was not that she first cultivated the path and attained enlightenment solely by means of a female form.

Since that "Wondrously Adorned One" (Miaozhuangyan) is neither designated as the king of a particular era nor described as being from a specific region, although her exhortation of women is not without some small benefit, there are nonetheless members of the monastic community who believe in and practice this wondrous scripture; for this reason, I have brought forth [this account].
King Longshu said: According to the Tripitaka, the hands, feet, and six sense organs of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are always upright;

hence they are called the "Eight Uprights. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is fundamentally seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), and his supernatural powers and transformations are sovereign and unimpeded.
Therefore, it is called Avalokiteśvara. That people nowadays depict him sitting with one leg raised and one hand resting on the knee, claiming this is the "Avalokita-Āryāvalokiteśvara," is an error.
